item.content:encoded:
We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. Elsewhere in the American League, the Guardians and White Sox are still battling for the division title, though the loser of that should slot into the third wild-card spot.
While all the divisions in the National League have been clinched already, the wild-card race, specifically in terms of seeding, is very much heating up, with the Phillies, Cubs and Padres entering play on Wednesday in a three-way tie.
Which clubs will get to keep playing into October? And which will watch their playoff aspirations come to an end?
Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we’ve seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Buster Olney and Jorge Castillo to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.
1. Milwaukee Brewers
Record: 99-59
Previous ranking: 1
With the season down to a handful of games, the Brewers have all but run out of time for Kyle Harrison to recover his first-half form. Harrison was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the break; he’s 2-3 with a 7.80 ERA since. His strikeout rate has remained steady, even as his velocity and movement measures have become more volatile. Meanwhile, his walk rate has more than doubled, and his homers-allowed rate has nearly tripled. Suffice to say, this is not a great combination of trends. Milwaukee has tried to get Harrison back in stride by using him out of the bullpen, but he’s gotten hammered as a reliever. Brewers fans who dreamed of a big three rotation of Jacob Misiorowski, Harrison and Logan Henderson probably need to recalibrate their expectations at this point. -- Doolittle
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Record: 97-61
Previous ranking: 2
We’re nearing October baseball, and it’s as if the Dodgers are knocking off items on a to-do list. Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup? Check. Edwin Diaz finding his stuff, finally? Check. Will Smith back in the lineup? Check -- and he has an OPS of close to 1.000 this month. Mookie Betts back to being Mookie Betts? Check. Kyle Tucker digging out of his seasonlong slump? Check. L.A. is putting the pieces back together just in time as it begins its effort to become the first NL team to go back-to-back-to-back. -- Olney
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Record: 96-62
Previous ranking: 3
Tampa Bay began the season with the longest odds to win the AL East. On Tuesday, it clinched its first division title since 2021 with a win over the Yankees. The Rays will enter their first postseason since 2023 as the favorites to win the AL pennant behind a distinct home-field advantage at Tropicana Field, a strong pitching staff and a dynamic lineup centered around MVP candidate Junior Caminero, designated hitter Yandy Diaz and first baseman Jonathan Aranda. With a payroll that ranks 28th in the majors, the Rays seek to become the team with the lowest-ranked payroll to ever win the World Series. -- Castillo
4. Atlanta Braves
Record: 93-65
Previous ranking: 5
Atlanta would’ve preferred to get a first-round bye in the playoffs, of course, but the fact that the Brewers and Dodgers seemed to have locked down the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds allows the Braves to treat this last week of the regular season like the last week of spring training. They can plot out the best way to rest their key relievers, assess the progress of Robert Suarez and arrange at-bats for the position players to be primed for the postseason. Meanwhile, the teams the Braves are likely to face in the first round -- the Phillies, Cubs and Padres -- are all still pushing for berths and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. -- Olney
5. New York Yankees
Record: 91-67
Previous ranking: 4
Despite manager Aaron Boone saying on Tuesday that Aaron Judge isn’t expected to return from his calf strain in time for the wild-card round, Judge told ESPN the following day that he does in fact intend to be ready for Game 1. He suffered the injury last Wednesday and was placed on the injured list two days later. The Yankees were initially cryptic about the setback, declining to disclose the severity and Judge’s outlook.
Boone offered some clarity Tuesday when he called it a “moderate strain” and acknowledged that the club does not plan on having him to open the postseason. Judge received a PPP injection Monday. The Yankees hope that will spur recovery. Otherwise, New York faces an uphill challenge to survive in October without its three-time MVP at his best. -- Castillo
6. Chicago Cubs
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 6
No player has made more of a second-half leap than Alex Bregman, whose season has just gathered momentum almost daily since the last week of July. That momentum was stopped in its tracks when Bregman suffered facial fractures last weekend when struck by a foul ball. The good news is that the Cubs decided against placing Bregman on the IL, believing he might be ready for the playoffs after.
But even if that proves to be optimistic, Cubs fans can take solace in the presence of icy-cool rookie Pedro Ramirez. The Cubs didn’t drop off much when Dansby Swanson was injured, as Ramirez provided a league-average bat and glove work at both second and third base that has kept an elite Cubs defense on track. You want Bregman in there, for sure -- but Ramirez provides a heck of a Plan B. -- Doolittle
7. San Diego Padres
Record: 88-70
Previous ranking: 8
San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot is shrinking, allowing general manager A.J. Preller and skipper Craig Stammen the chance to line up their staff for the wild-card series, with options developing. Stammen indicated to reporters that unless Michael King is needed to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the regular season, he will be held over to start Game 1 of the wild card, wherever that is -- so he wouldn’t necessarily be used Sunday in order to win home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs.
Additionally, the Padres are in a better position to rest their bullpen, the perceived strength of the team. Adrian Morejon ranks third among all relievers in innings. Rest might be overrated for Mason Miller: He has made 16 appearances on zero days’ rest, and in those games, he has allowed two hits and one earned run in 16⅔ innings, with two walks and 27 strikeouts. -- Olney
8. Philadelphia Phillies
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 7
The culture of Philadelphia’s starting pitchers, from Zack Wheeler to Cristopher Sanchez to Aaron Nola, is to pitch deep into games. Unlike so many starters in this generation, Wheeler takes the mound expecting to work into the late innings -- and the Phillies will need this sort of production from the rotation, given the team’s recent bullpen problems. Orion Kerkering, an important part of the relief corps, struggled so badly that he was sent to the minors last week. Jose Alvarado has pitched better down the stretch, and hard-throwing Alex MacFarlane has quickly ascended into an important role in his rookie season in the bullpen. But the Phillies’ rotation will carry the team’s October dreams. -- Olney
9. Boston Red Sox
Record: 85-73
Previous ranking: 9
The Red Sox rewarded Chad Tracy on Tuesday for leading the team’s historic turnaround by removing his interim tag and giving him a three-year contract to continue as manager. Now he’ll look to accomplish what his predecessor Alex Cora couldn’t last year: beating the Yankees on the road in the AL Wild Card Series.
Boston has cooled off since going 32-5 to put itself in playoff position and faces some injury uncertainty going into October. Ceddanne Rafaela returned Tuesday after missing 16 games with a quad injury, and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand last Thursday and is dealing with soreness. On the mound, the Red Sox could receive two significant reinforcements for the bullpen in Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck. Crochet, last season’s AL Cy Young runner-up, has been out with a shoulder injury since late April, while Houck hasn’t appeared in a game in 2026. -- Castillo
10. Cleveland Guardians
Record: 82-76
Previous ranking: 12
Cleveland is, once again, showing its knack for a strong finishing kick. Over the past decade, only the Dodgers have won more September games. For Guardians fans aching for their team’s first title since the Truman administration, October is a higher priority at this point.
Like the White Sox, the first order of business is to secure the AL Central title and the first-round bye likely to go with it. Given the neck-and-neck nature of Cleveland’s battle with Chicago, there likely isn’t going to be much time for manager Stephen Vogt to ease up on the pedal to finish the season. That would be nice to do when it comes to rookie ace Parker Messick, who will finish the season with at least 50 more innings than he has ever thrown in a season. Messick has shown no signs of fatigue, so it may not matter. -- Doolittle
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-74
Previous ranking: 10
Manager Torey Lovullo’s comments in a radio interview last week in which he acknowledged that the Diamondbacks “probably” -- his word -- need to reach the postseason to earn him a contract extension surprised many in the industry, as Lovullo has a strong and long-standing relationship with his boss, Mike Hazen. The Ketel Marte situation has been challenging for the organization, with the team’s highest-paid position player failing to show up to the park, and owner Ken Kendrick has a reputation for being mercurial and demanding. Lovullo’s contract runs out at season’s end, and he and the Diamondbacks agreed they would discuss his status then. -- Olney
12. Chicago White Sox
Record: 81-77
Previous ranking: 11
The White Sox have wobbled down the stretch, but they have not fallen down. It looks like they will join the playoff party, completing an incredible two-year turnaround that saw them go from setting the modern single-season loss record to playing in October.
Barring a face-plant over the last few days of the season, the question of whether the Sox can overtake Cleveland for the AL Central title is the biggest remaining question. It’s impactful, with a first-round bye likely on the line. A bye is a boon for any team, but among likely postseason entrants, it might loom largest for the White Sox. That’s just because of how manager Will Venable has had to stretch his pitching resources to the maximum just to get to this point. A wild-card skip would give his staff at least a little time to regroup before the ALDS begins. -- Doolittle
13. Pittsburgh Pirates
Record: 80-78
Previous ranking: 14
Why did Paul Skenes lapse into baseball’s pitching middle class rather than continue his march toward Cooperstown? There is no bigger task for the Pirates and Skenes this offseason than figuring this out. With one more start to go, he has already allowed more runs this season than he did in his first two seasons combined. To be sure, it’s not all on Skenes, whose expected ERA, 3.27 per Statcast, is unusually divergent from his actual ERA (3.91). Still, even a 3.27 ERA is a far cry from the level of effectiveness Skenes flashed before this season. Why? Finding the answer to that question could prove to be the biggest addition Pittsburgh makes this winter. -- Doolittle
14. Texas Rangers
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 16
With eyes on the disappointing Mariners and Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown watch, the Rangers quietly remained in contention in the historically dreadful AL West all summer. Following three straight losses, they now find themselves tied atop the division with Houston. Texas will host the Mets in a series finale Thursday before finishing the season with three games in Minnesota. The Rangers will need to finish with a better record than the Astros, who own the tiebreaker, to reach the postseason for the first time since winning the 2023 World Series. -- Castillo
15. Houston Astros
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 13
The Astros fired general manager Dana Brown last month and are under .500 with four games remaining ... but they still have a real chance to win the division. That’s the AL West in 2026. The Astros finish the regular season with a four-game series in West Sacramento against an A’s team that has an MLB-worst run differential. The bad news: The Astros head there tied atop the division. The good news: They hold the tiebreaker over Texas. In the background over the last few days of the season: Alvarez’s push to become the first player to win a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2013. -- Castillo
16. Toronto Blue Jays
Record: 77-82
Previous ranking: 15
The Blue Jays did not replicate their 2025 magic in 2026, largely due to injuries and their offense falling off a cliff. They finished last season fourth in the majors with a 112 wRC+; this season, they’re tied for 24th with a 95 wRC+. The dropoff starts with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer. Guerrero has nine home runs -- and, inexplicably, just one at home -- with a .695 OPS in the first year of a 14-year, $500 million contract extension. Springer, who reversed a precipitous decline to hit 32 home runs with a .959 OPS last season, has 15 home runs with a .730 OPS in 124 games this year -- and he’s a free agent after this season. Whether Springer re-signs or not, a rebound in 2027 starts with Guerrero sparking an offense that is tied for last in home runs in 2026. -- Castillo
17. Miami Marlins
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 18
Here’s the good news about the Marlins’ 2026 season: They hung around all year, battling among the contenders and having some individual successes. Here’s what’s not-so-great about where they stand right now: It’s hard to identify the players who could lead a Miami breakout into full-scale contention with the best NL teams.
Otto Lopez had an excellent season, but he’ll turn 28 years old next week and his OPS is under .800. Griffin Conine is the one player on the team with an OPS over .800, and he’s 29. Sandy Alcantara reestablished himself as a rotation leader, but he’s 31. Eury Perez has flashes of dominance and is just 23, but he’s got an injury history and will finish this season with an ERA over 4.00. More depth and more talent is needed for the Marlins to take the next step. -- Olney
18. Baltimore Orioles
Record: 78-81
Previous ranking: 19
Another disappointing season in Baltimore has already prompted some changes in the front office, but not at the top. President of baseball operations Mike Elias is expected to return in 2027. One move his front office got right was signing Pete Alonso last winter. The first baseman, who has played in every game this season, hit his 40th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays. He clearly isn’t why the Orioles aren’t going to the postseason for the second straight year.
Baltimore’s young position player core has not lived up to the hype, while the pitching staff wasn’t good enough to shoulder the load. Elias & Co. already decided to move on from former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, an All-Star catcher previously considered a foundational player, at the trade deadline. More significant moves could come this offseason. -- Castillo
19. St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 77-81
Previous ranking: 17
This rebuilding season has been an unqualified success for the Cardinals. If not for a leaky bullpen, their soft wild-card contention might have been a lot more solid. While bullpens are sometimes the final piece of the contention puzzle for a building team, that’s not always the case. Some clubs develop a bullpen-building process that takes effect even as the rest of the roster remains a work in progress. The Pirates of recent vintage are a good example.
Thus, the project of putting together a contention-worthy bullpen is a crucial one for the Chaim Bloom-led front office. Bloom was part of a Rays front office that annually churned out elite, no-name bullpens. However, during the four years that Bloom led the Red Sox front office, Boston ranked 24th in bullpen ERA (4.48) and middle-of-the-pack in save percentage. Good first year, but there is more to prove in St. Louis. -- Doolittle
20. Detroit Tigers
Record: 74-85
Previous ranking: 20
The Tigers will probably finish fourth in the AL in run differential, perhaps third if they pass the Red Sox, and will easily pace the Central by that measure. When you consider that, along with Detroit’s freakishly bad record in one- and two-run games (now 21-51) and the relatively short list of players on expiring deals (Jack Flaherty and Gleyber Torres, along with the retiring Justin Verlander), the Tigers are an obvious and very strong bounce-back candidate for the 2027 season. That doesn’t mean that president of baseball operations Scott Harris and his staff don’t have their work cut out for them when it comes to evaluating this lackluster season. Still, for the Tigers’ disappointed fans, it’s important to keep in mind that their team will be proceeding from a relative position of strength. -- Doolittle
21. Washington Nationals
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 23
In so many ways, the 2026 season was a success for the Nationals, who exceeded expectations this year, flirting with contention in the first half and seeing the development of players like CJ Abrams and James Wood into offensive stars. But the team’s pitching collapsed in the second half -- Washington’s second-half ERA of 4.49 ranks 25th. The Nationals locked down Cade Cavalli to a multiyear deal last week at the end of what has been a breakout season, but it’s clear that president of baseball operations Paul Toboni’s greatest challenge is to develop the sort of pipeline of pitching that will allow them to compete with the big-market teams in the division. -- Olney
22. Seattle Mariners
Record: 74-84
Previous ranking: 24
A year after falling one win short of the franchise’s first World Series appearance, the Mariners’ season will end Sunday with a whimper. The 2026 campaign will be remembered as the most disappointing one in franchise history.
Cal Raleigh’s drop-off from 60 home runs and an MVP runner-up finish was baffling. Julio Rodriguez regressed and still hasn’t made the superstar jump widely expected of him. Josh Naylor was a below-average hitter in the first year of his five-year contract. The starting rotation was not as good as advertised. Changes are inevitable, likely starting with manager Dan Wilson. But the Mariners can’t fire all of their players. They’ll need their core to bounce back from down seasons in order to rebound in 2027. -- Castillo
23. New York Mets
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 21
No one will go into the 2027 season under more pressure than David Stearns, the Mets’ head of baseball operations, following their collapse down the stretch in 2025 and the poor 2026 season. So it makes sense that he worked to keep someone he has a working relationship with in the managerial role, Andy Green, who had his interim tag removed and was hired to a three-year deal Tuesday. Steve Cohen’s comments on an SNY broadcast about needing new voices within the organization got the attention of a lot of rival executives, who wondered if the impact of Pete Alonso’s encore performance at Citi Field and the “Fire Stearns” chants last week made an impression on the owner. Under the circumstances, hiring Green seems like the right move for Stearns, the smart move. -- Olney
24. Minnesota Twins
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 22
The arrival of prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez has the Twins’ prospective 2027 position group in good shape even if veteran Josh Bell declines his mutual option and departs. The murkiest position is catcher, where Ryan Jeffers is likely headed for free agency, presumably after the Twins issue him a qualifying offer. The QO could limit Jeffers’ market, but probably not that much, as Jeffers looks like the best free agent catcher option out there. If he leaves, the Twins will need someone to pair with Caratini.
Long term, after drafting Vahn Lackey third in the most recent draft, the Twins seem in good shape with him, Eduardo Tait, Khadim Diaw and Carson Tinney all showing well in prospect rankings. Alas, none of that quartet is likely to be a 2027 solution. -- Doolittle
25. Cincinnati Reds
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 25
The ongoing maturation of Elly De La Cruz, as he edges toward his career prime, has provided ample reason to keep an eye on the Reds, even amid a last-place showing. Still, there have been enough trade rumors regarding the supremely talented shortstop to make you wonder just how long De La Cruz will be around.
Recent comments made by his agent, Scott Boras, don’t help. Boras suggested to reporters that a future foray into the open market made more sense for De La Cruz than a below-market extension. What does that mean for the Reds in the near term? For now, he has three more years of team control, so there’s no reason to be rash. Still, with this cloud starting to form over Great American Park, some sort of clarity about how the Reds plan to deal with their best player would be nice. -- Doolittle
26. Kansas City Royals
Record: 68-90
Previous ranking: 26
The Royals’ biggest offseason project will be to figure out their 2027 bullpen formula. That process begins with evaluating the relievers already on hand. Presumed closer Carlos Estevez had shoulder surgery -- bafflingly not until the second week of September -- and the Royals almost certainly won’t pick up their 2027 club option on him. Lucas Erceg looked lost before being shipped off to Omaha, but he performed well in Triple-A and his velocity upon his return to the majors has been at its highest level all year. Which Erceg is the real one? Is journeyman righty Nate Pearson a leverage option? Does Craig Kimbrel have anything left? The Royals will need relief help from outside the organization, but how much of it will depend on the outcome of these evaluations and others. -- Doolittle
27. San Francisco Giants
Record: 65-94
Previous ranking: 27
The general perception of San Francisco’s farm system is that it improved in 2026, and Bryce Eldridge established himself as a player the organization could build around. Beyond that, however, the Giants really haven’t progressed. They have a top-heavy payroll situation, with hundreds of millions owed to Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman. The questions about manager Tony Vitello making the jump from college to professional baseball weren’t quelled by his first season with the Giants -- and neither were the questions about the man who hired him, Buster Posey, who is still relatively new to his front office role. -- Olney
28. Athletics
Record: 63-95
Previous ranking: 28
The A’s are stumbling to the finish line having lost 95 games. All-Star catcher Shea Langeliers recently returned from knee surgery, but several other prominent players remain on the IL, including Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, Jacob Wilson, Brent Rooker, Luis Severino and Gage Jump. They’ll enter their season-ending series against the Astros with a negative-217 run differential -- the worst in the majors by 33 runs. With one season remaining before the A’s move to Las Vegas in 2028, they enter the winter in search of a general manager after David Forst’s departure in early August. Their offseason priorities are straightforward: Get healthy and improve a pitching staff that has a 5.43 ERA (29th) despite pitching half its games at the launchpad known as Sutter Health Park. -- Castillo
29. Los Angeles Angels
Record: 60-98
Previous ranking: 29
The Angels, despite 11 straight losing seasons, are the only franchise in the majors that has yet to post a 100-loss season. That could change this weekend in Seattle, where the Angels will need to win three of four games to avoid reaching the century mark. It’d be a fitting conclusion to Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner. Last month, Moreno agreed to sell controlling interest in the team to Stan Kroenke for a record valuation of $4 billion. Kroenke will take over a franchise that has not appeared in the postseason since 2014 and has not won a postseason game since 2009.
The first order of business this offseason will be hiring fired general manager Perry Minasian’s replacement. The team could also be in search of a manager to replace Kurt Suzuki, who is on a one-year contract. It is a transformative time in Anaheim. -- Castillo
30. Colorado Rockies
Record: 57-101
Previous ranking: 30
Colorado has compiled 100 losses for the fourth consecutive season; the last team to suffer 100-plus losses in five consecutive seasons were the Phillies, from 1938 to 1942. In Paul DePodesta’s first year of running Colorado’s baseball operations, there were some under-the-hood improvements: the biggest run differential improvement of all 30 teams in 2026, an improved farm system and some nice finds for the every-day lineup, like Jake McCarthy, TJ Rumfield and Connor Norby. There’s still a long way to go to competitive relevance for the Rockies, especially given the high bar required in the Dodgers’ NL West. -- Olney

item.title: [Bleacher Report] 2026 MLB Awards Picks For AL and NL MVP, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year, Every Major Award
item.dc:creator: Kerry Miller

But if you're not that patient, we can go ahead and unofficially declare those winners now. For the most part, this year's awards races have been pretty boring. Shohei Ohtani vs. Pete Crow-Armstrong for NL MVP was a fun debate for about a week, b
item.content:encoded:
2026 MLB Awards Picks For AL and NL MVP, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year, Every Major Award
We'll have to wait until mid-November to officially find out who wins Major League Baseball's Most Valuable Player, Cy Young and Rookie of the Year awards for 2026.
But if you're not that patient, we can go ahead and unofficially declare those winners now.
For the most part, this year's awards races have been pretty boring. Shohei Ohtani vs. Pete Crow-Armstrong for NL MVP was a fun debate for about a week, but PCA is probably going to win unanimously at this point. That might also be true for AL MVP, both Cy Youngs and maybe even both Rookies of the Year.
At any rate, there's nothing even remotely close to last year's Aaron Judge vs. Cal Raleigh debate.
For each of those six awards, though, who is most likely to finish as first runner-up? Who has slipped through the cracks and not gotten nearly as much attention as they deserve?
Before we get into those big six, we'll start with a few much more debatable awards, like Manager and Comeback Player of the Year.
Statistics current through the start of play on Wednesday.
Comeback Player of the Year
1 of 10
AL CPOY: Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros
MLB has been officially naming a comeback player of the year in each league on an annual basis since 2005. The only player thus far to win both this award and MVP in the same season was Buster Posey in 2012. Alvarez is destined for both trophies after playing in just 48 games with a sub-.800 OPS in 2025. Not only has he bounced back, but he has been better than ever before.
Also Worth Considering: Shane McClanahan, Gerrit Cole, Mike Trout, Willson Contreras, Nick Martinez
NL CPOY: Sandy Alcantara, Miami Marlins
Of all the awards we'll get into today, this one is the toughest to pick.
Zack Wheeler deserves serious consideration for a dominant return from thoracic outlet syndrome surgery. However, because he merely missed the final six weeks of last season and the first four weeks of the current campaign, he might get overlooked.
Eduardo Rodriguez was dreadful over the past two seasons, posting an ERA north of 5.00 in each, but he is under 3.00 this season and is the biggest reason the Diamondbacks have made it this far with a postseason pulse.
Michael Harris II has also had a major bounce back from a disappointing 2025.
If you possibly had Ty France penciled in as San Diego's best hitter in 2026 after four separate teams in the previous two years sent him packing with a sub-.700 OPS, please step forward to claim your prize.
Alcantara probably takes the cake for returning to his throne as the rubber-armed ace of the Marlins. He missed all of 2024 following Tommy John surgery and had a horrendous first four months of last season. He returned to his old self this year, leading the majors in innings pitched with a sub-4.00 ERA.
Also Considered: Zack Wheeler, Eduardo Rodriguez, Ty France, Michael Harris II, Nolan Arenado, Garrett Mitchell, Tanner Scott
Reliever of the Year
2 of 10
AL Reliever of the Year: Louis Varland, Toronto Blue Jays
It was clear from last October that the Blue Jays had a lot of faith in Varland, using him in a record-setting 15 postseason games. He did so with a 3.94 ERA. He entered 2026 with a career 4.66 ERA during the regular season and nary a save in his big-league career.
This year, though, he was pretty much forced into the closer role in late April by Jeff Hoffman's struggles and subsequently became the king of the ninth inning, going 34-for-36 in save chances with a 1.29 ERA in 77 innings pitched.
Also Worth Considering: Cade Smith, Bryan Baker, Paul Blackburn, Jacob Latz
NL Reliever of the Year: Mason Miller, San Diego Padres
Varland winning the AL award would have been unthinkable six months ago, but Miller doing so in the NL was the expectation all along.
Miller was special from the outset with the Athletics, but getting traded to the Padres last summer unlocked a whole new level of dominance. Between his 85 regular season and two postseason appearances with San Diego, he has a 1.06 ERA, a 0.78 WHIP and a 17.0 K/9.
He has gone 37-for-40 in save chances this season, with two of the three blown saves coming in a "break in case of emergency" situation, with the winning run already on base and one out in the eighth inning. Even then, he pitched well enough that the Padres still won after the save was blown.
Also Worth Considering: Jhoan Duran, Adrian Morejon, Tanner Scott, Didier Fuentes
Manager of the Year
3 of 10
AL Manager of the Year: Kevin Cash, Tampa Bay Rays
Chad Tracy gets a serious tip o' the cap for inheriting a mess from Alex Cora in late April and rallying the troops for a postseason berth.
However, Boston was supposed to be good and maybe needed that change of guard to eventually turn things around. Tampa Bay, on the other hand, was supposed to finish in dead last in the AL East, given a preseason win total of 76.5.
Thanks to Cash's leadership in the dugout, bets on the over cashed more than a month ago, as the Rays have already locked up the American League's No. 1 seed.
(If this award goes to Will Venable, though, no arguments here. Can't imagine there are many, if any, instances in history of a manager improving a team by at least 19 wins in back-to-back seasons, let alone in his first two years as a big-league manager.)
Also Worth Considering: Chad Tracy, Boston Red Sox; Will Venable, Chicago White Sox
NL Manager of the Year: Pat Murphy, Milwaukee Brewers
Like Tracy in Boston, three cheers to Don Mattingly in Philadelphia for taking over a 9-19 disaster in late April before steering the Phillies (barring a disaster scenario in this closing stretch) back to the postseason.
Mattingly merely got them back onto the right track, though, headed for a photo finish on that 89.5 preseason win total. Murphy should be headed for a third straight NL Manager of the Year award for repeatedly raising the bar in Milwaukee.
The Brewers set a franchise record with 97 wins last season. They've already reset that record this year.
Despite trading away three of last year's 10 most valuable players (Freddy Peralta, Caleb Durbin and Isaac Collins) during the winter.
Despite having last year's breakout pitcher, Quinn Priester, land on the IL in spring training and never return.
Despite losing Brandon Woodruff to a season-ending shoulder injury after just nine appearances.
And despite Christian Yelich dropping off a cliff for career-worst numbers.
Mattingly helped revive the Phillies, but Murphy might actually be a magician.
Also Worth Considering: Don Mattingly, Philadelphia Phillies
Platinum Gloves
4 of 10
AL Platinum Glove: Bobby Witt Jr., Kansas City Royals
Witt also received this honor last season, when he was a tiny bit better and a good bit healthier.
Unless it's going to Dillon Dingler for proving that the art of framing pitches still matters in the ABS era, Witt ought to be the repeat winner of the American League's Platinum Glove.
It feels like a lifetime ago that he was a liability on defense as a rookie, but he has blossomed into one of the best five-tool players in the game today. He is sure to finish top seven in the AL MVP vote for a fourth straight year.
Also Worth Considering: Dillon Dingler, Detroit Tigers; Ceddanne Rafaela, Boston Red Sox; Ezequiel Duran, Texas Rangers
NL Platinum Glove: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Chicago Cubs
The quest for a 40/40 season has drawn all the attention around PCA, but his range in center field might be even more ludicrous than what he is accomplishing on offense.
As a result, he makes the improbable look routine and makes the impossible look anything but.
Crow-Armstrong has gone 8-for-16 on 5-star catch opportunities. He is the only qualified outfielder north of 30 percent (let alone 50 percent) in that category. He is also 12-for-15 on 4-star catch opportunities for a combined total of 20 catches and a 64.5 percent success rate on plays with a catch probability of 50 percent or lower. No other player has more than 13 such catches. AJ Ewing (6-for-7 on 4-star; 2-for-9 on 5-star; 50 percent total) is the only other with a success rate of 38 percent or better.
That's a lot of numbers to say that if anyone is going to replicate Willie Mays' iconic catch in the 1954 World Series, it's PCA. (He may well also homer and steal a bag while he's at it.)
Also Worth Considering: JJ Wetherholt, St. Louis Cardinals
AL Rookie of the Year
5 of 10
Who Will Win: Kevin McGonigle, Detroit Tigers
It's wild to think McGonigle has been worth more wins above replacement than any other hitter in the American League, even though he hadn't made his Double-A debut until 15 months ago.
It's also wild to think Detroit couldn't even sniff the postseason in this year's American League while getting such a remarkable season from its 21-year-old infielder, but he certainly did everything in his power to keep the Tigers afloat.
At the moment, McGonigle has drawn 94 walks against 95 strikeouts. If he can get that ratio back up to 1.00 or better, he would become the first player to do so in an age-21-or-younger campaign with at least 400 plate appearances since Gary Sheffield in 1990.
Worthiest Challenger: Parker Messick, Cleveland Guardians
McGonigle might win in unanimous fashion, but Messick hasn't had an ERA north of 3.00 at any point in this entire season and really ought to be a more serious threat in this race. In starts in which Messick received at least three runs of support, Cleveland has gone 18-3. They might end up with a first-round bye because of it.
Deserved More Attention: Walbert Ureña, Los Angeles Angels
NL Rookie of the Year
6 of 10
Who Will Win: Sal Stewart, Cincinnati Reds
Of the six races for major awards, NL ROY is the most debatable by far.
Whether you prefer Baseball-Reference or FanGraphs for your sabermetrics, JJ Wetherholt has Sal Stewart smoked in wins above replacement.
At a certain point, the RBI count matters more than the WAR calculation, as evidenced by the fact that all seven rookies to tally at least 111 RBI in a season over the past seven decades were named Rookie of the Year, four of them in unanimous fashion.
What's wild about Stewart sitting one shy of that plateau is that the Reds rank dead last in the National League in scoring. He has made the most of his opportunities, though, batting .301/.361/.569 with runners in scoring position. Because of that, there's a chance he's going to lead the majors in RBI.
Worthiest Challenger: JJ Wetherholt, St. Louis Cardinals
Wetherholt has had a preposterously impressive season in the field, last committing an error on April 10. Pete Crow-Armstrong will probably win the NL's Platinum Glove, but this rookie is the one player who could plausibly prevent that. Though a ton of his value added stems from his defense, the Cardinals aren't exactly hiding his bat in the lineup, batting him leadoff in every game that he has started.
Deserved More Attention: Logan Henderson, Milwaukee Brewers
AL Cy Young
7 of 10
Who Will Win: Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees
From 1972 to 2025, there were 12 cases of a pitcher recording at least 225 strikeouts with a sub-2.00 ERA and a sub-1.00 WHIP.
All 12 of them won the Cy Young Award. Cam Schlittler and Jacob Misiorowski will be joining that fraternity soon.
Schlittler has made 24 starts in which he allowed zero or one earned run and 24 starts in which he had at least as many strikeouts as the number of baserunners allowed.
The four-seamer is his moneymaker, responsible for more than half of his strikeouts. His sinker has been just as deadly. Opponents are hitting below .180 and slugging below .270 against both of those occasionally-more-than-100 MPH offerings.
Worthiest Challenger: Dylan Cease, Toronto Blue Jays
This was quite the two-horse race until about three weeks ago, when Cease's diminishing velocity started producing diminishing returns. Through the end of August, though, he was striking out 36.1 percent of opposing hitters, which is better than where Justin Verlander, Max Scherzer or Clayton Kershaw ever finished a season. For the Blue Jays' sake, here's hoping his shoulder inflammation doesn't turn into anything more long-lasting.
Deserved More Attention: Gavin Williams, Cleveland Guardians
NL Cy Young
8 of 10
Who Will Win: Jacob Misiorowski, Milwaukee Brewers
The Miz was to 2026 what Paul Skenes was to the 2024 and 2025 campaigns: appointment-viewing television every time he stepped on the mound.
The magnum opus was his 15-strikeout, one-hit shutout of the Phillies in mid-June. But his biggest "I beg your pardon, he's doing what now?" performance came against Colorado in late July, in which he struck out 12 of the first 13 batters he faced.
Unfortunately, that was his second start back after missing a bit of time with arm fatigue, so we all knew he wasn't going to pitch deep enough into the game to break the single-game strikeout record. Still, it was one of the most dominant abbreviated starts in recent memory and a sobering reminder of how untouchable Misiorowski can be when he's in his bag.
Worthiest Challenger: Cristopher Sánchez, Philadelphia Phillies
Atlanta's Chris Sale might actually finish second in this vote with his 2.18 ERA. However, while Atlanta pretty much always gave Sale at least five days' rest en route to just barely qualifying for the ERA title, Sánchez has been a workhorse, going at least 200 innings for the second straight year. Though May feels like ancient history at this point, that scoreless streak of 50.2 innings pitched was a legendary run.
Deserved More Attention: Jesús Luzardo, Philadelphia Phillies
AL MVP
9 of 10
Who Will Win: Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros
If you want your MVP to be a five-tool guy, Alvarez isn't for you. He almost ranks dead last in the majors in baserunning run value, per Baseball Savant. While logging just 186.0 innings in left field—several pitchers have spent more time in the field than that—he committed multiple errors.
Also, if you want the MVP to be the best player on the best team, go ahead and scroll down a bit to Junior Caminero instead. Alvarez definitively has been Houston's most valuable player, but the Astros are a game below .500 and fighting to even reach the postseason.
With just five games left, though, Alvarez is the overwhelming favorite for AL MVP because he is leading the majors in batting average, on-base percentage and slugging percentage. No one has drawn more walks. Only Pete Crow-Armstrong has more total bases.
If he ends up one home run or one RBI shy of the Triple Crown, maybe we can retroactively award him a solo shot for that "foul ball" that he hammered off the rafters on Opening Day?
Worthiest Challenger: Junior Caminero, Tampa Bay Rays
In case you thought Caminero's 45-homer campaign last year was a "benefited from playing home games at a spring training venue" fluke, he doubled down with an even more impressive run through 2026. Not quite as many home runs, but he did join 1953-54 Eddie Mathews as the only hitters in MLB history with multiple seasons of 40+ home runs by the end of their age-22 season. Caminero also improved his on-base percentage by 50 points, becoming more of an overall asset at the dish.
Deserved More Attention: Miguel Vargas, Chicago White Sox
NL MVP
10 of 10
Who Will Win: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Chicago Cubs
What's bonkers about Crow-Armstrong now running away with the NL MVP and one swipe away from the 40/40 club is that it seemed impossible four months ago.
In late May, most of the discourse about PCA involved a couple of careless errors in center field, his disappointing sub-.700 OPS or that profane altercation with a White Sox fan. Through 58 games, he was hitting .224 with six home runs and 12 stolen bases. Trea Turner (.222, seven and 11, respectively) was in pretty much the exact same boat. We're still waiting on him to snap out of his funk.
Since May 30, though, Crow-Armstrong has triple-slashed .312/.404/.693 while operating at 162-game paces of 64 home runs and 44 stolen bases.
Even if Shohei Ohtani hadn't gotten hurt, PCA's run to a possible 10 WAR season probably would've been enough to win this vote.
Worthiest Challenger: Shohei Ohtani, Los Angeles Dodgers
Season Stats: .277/.380/.522, 30 HR, 80 RBI, 11 SB; 85.2 IP, 1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 10.0 K/9, 6.5 bWAR
Ohtani is one of three hitters with at least 30 home runs and an OPS of .900 or better. The others are inevitable MVPs Alvarez and PCA. Ohtani is also one of three pitchers with at least 80 innings, a sub-2.00 ERA and a sub-1.00 WHIP. The others are inevitable Cy Youngs Schlittler and Misiorowski. He hasn't pitched since early July and hasn't been the same hitter since early August. But if you've been disappointed by Ohtani's season, you might want to recalibrate.
Deserved More Attention: Elly De La Cruz, Cincinnati Reds

item.content:encoded:
Inspired by this year’s lowly AL West, here are the weakest teams to make MLB’s postseason
Posted/updated on: September 24, 2026 at 6:59 am
With just a few days left in the regular season, the AL West might make a particularly mediocre kind of history.
After Tuesday night’s games, the Texas Rangers and Houston Astros were tied for first place at 78-79. No full-season division champion has ever had a losing record.
In fact, no team has made the postseason with a sub-.500 record, unless you count a trio of participants from years the playoffs were temporarily expanded: In the 2020 season shortened by the COVID-19 pandemic, Milwaukee and Houston were both 29-31 and made the postseason. In 1981, the Kansas City Royals went 50-53 overall — but they were the AL West’s top team in the post-strike second half, meaning they got in.
MLB expanded its postseason to 12 teams in 2022, raising the likelihood that a sub-.500 team would sneak into October at some point. Just a few weeks ago, it looked like the American League could have several clubs with losing marks in this year’s playoffs. The AL Central’s Cleveland Guardians and Chicago White Sox have since reached 81 wins, so that won’t happen. But the AL West title race could still yield a losing team.
In honor of that, here are 10 of the weakest teams to make the postseason, listed in chronological order with their records and run differentials in mind. Note that some of them went on lengthy postseason runs — so don’t count out the Rangers or Astros just yet.
1973 New York Mets
Record: 82-79 (first in NL East)
Run differential: 20
Postseason: Beat Cincinnati 3-2 in NL Championship Series, lost to Oakland 4-3 in World Series
The rallying cry was “Ya gotta believe!” from reliever Tug McGraw. It wasn’t easy when New York was in last place after an Aug. 30 loss, but the Mets went 21-8 the rest of the way to win the division by 1 1/2 games. Tom Seaver (19-10, 2.08 ERA, 18 complete games) was still at the peak of his powers, and New York held the Reds to eight runs in five games in the NLCS — a series best remembered for a brawl involving Bud Harrelson and Pete Rose. The Mets led the World Series 3-2 and had Seaver starting Game 6, but they couldn’t close out the Athletics.
1984 Kansas City Royals
Record: 84-78 (first in AL West)
Run differential: minus-13
Postseason: Lost to Detroit 3-0 in ALCS
The Royals were 11 games under .500 in the middle of July, but they did enough to win the AL West. George Brett hit .284 — his worst average in a 14-year span from 1975-88 — and he was one of just two All-Stars on the team. The other was Dan Quisenberry, who had 44 saves while throwing 129 1/3 innings. He finished second in the Cy Young race behind fellow reliever Willie Hernández of the Tigers. Although Kansas City took the division almost by default in ’84, the Royals improved to 91 wins the following year and won the World Series.
1987 Minnesota Twins
Record: 85-77 (first in AL West)
Run differential: minus-20
Postseason: Beat Detroit 4-1 in ALCS, beat St. Louis 4-3 in World Series
Frank Viola was the star of a pitching staff that otherwise offered little — aside from a trio of big names on the downside of their careers. Bert Blyleven allowed 46 home runs, Joe Niekro posted a 6.26 ERA and Steve Carlton made seven largely woeful starts for this Minnesota team. The Twins could hit, though. Kirby Puckett was third in the MVP race, while Kent Hrbek, Gary Gaetti and Tom Brunansky each surpassed 30 homers. Home-field advantage wasn’t determined by record back then, so Minnesota had it in the ALCS despite finishing 13 games behind the Tigers, and again in the World Series after being 10 games worse than the Cardinals. The Twins went 6-0 at the Metrodome in the postseason.
1995 Colorado Rockies
Record: 77-67 (second in NL West, wild card)
Run differential: 2
Postseason: Lost 3-1 to Atlanta in NL Division Series
The first wild card in National League history was this Colorado team in a season shortened by the end of the 1994-95 work stoppage. The Rockies’ ERA of 4.97 is the worst of the live ball era by a postseason team in a non-DH league. Colorado made up for that, not surprisingly, by leading the NL in runs. Dante Bichette led the league in home runs and RBIs and finished third in batting average.
2005 San Diego Padres
Record: 82-80 (first in NL West)
Run differential: minus-42
Postseason: Lost 3-0 to St. Louis in NLDS
Jake Peavy and a Trevor Hoffman-led bullpen helped San Diego reach the playoffs, but this team never looked the part. The Padres scored the fourth-fewest runs in all of baseball, and their starters went 52-60 with a 4.49 ERA. In the postseason, San Diego never had the lead at any point against the 100-win Cardinals. Game 1 was 8-0 after six innings, Game 2 was 6-1 after seven, and Game 3 was 7-0 after 4 1/2.
2006 St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 83-78 (first in NL Central)
Run differential: 19
Postseason: Beat San Diego 3-1 in NLDS, beat New York Mets 4-3 in NLCS, beat Detroit 4-1 in World Series
The Cardinals won at least 95 games four times under Tony La Russa, but their best postseason success came as a wild card in 2011 and with this team five years earlier. St. Louis nearly blew a seven-game lead in the division in the final two weeks of the regular season, but a roster with Albert Pujols, Scott Rolen, Chris Carpenter and a young reliever named Adam Wainwright always had a chance to get hot. Yadier Molina’s homer — and Wainwright’s strikeout of Carlos Beltrán — gave the Cardinals the pennant in an epic series with the Mets.
2017 Minnesota Twins
Record: 85-77 (second in AL Central, second wild card)
Run differential: 27
Postseason: Lost to New York Yankees in wild card game
After 103 losses in 2016, the Twins were in first place for a little while before eventually capturing the AL’s final postseason spot and losing 8-4 to the Yankees. Byron Buxton played 140 games, the most of his career to date, and Brian Dozier hit 34 home runs. Joe Mauer had moved to first base by this point but was still quite good at the plate, batting .305. Ervin Santana led the rotation in his last good major league season. This team certainly wasn’t great, but it was good enough in an AL that produced only five teams above .500.
2023 Miami Marlins
Record: 84-78 (third in NL East, second wild card)
Run differential: minus-57
Postseason: Lost to Philadelphia 2-0 in NL Wild Card Series
The Marlins posted the worst run differential to date by a postseason team — this year’s Astros are currently at minus-59 — but Miami went 33-14 in one-run games. The pitching staff with Sandy Alcantara, Eury Pérez, Jesús Luzardo and Braxton Garrett helped Miami into the playoffs. Of the Marlins’ top 12 players in plate appearances, seven of them finished with negative wins above replacement, according to Baseball Reference. The offense was basically batting champ Luis Arraez, designated hitter Jorge Soler and not much else. Miami lost 93 games the year before this playoff appearance and 100 the year after.
2023 Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-78 (second in NL West, third wild card)
Run differential: minus-15
Postseason: Beat Milwaukee 2-0 in NLWCS, beat Los Angeles Dodgers 3-0 in NLDS, beat Philadelphia 4-3 in NLCS, lost to Texas 4-1 in World Series
Just get in and anything can happen. These Diamondbacks were one of the best examples of that. Arizona started August with nine straight losses to fall below .500, but after doing enough to make the playoffs, they swept two division champions and then won the last two games of the NLCS on the road to capture the second pennant in franchise history. Arizona had a negative run differential in the regular season and was also outscored 30-21 in that series against the Phillies. It didn’t matter.
2025 Cincinnati Reds
Record: 83-79 (third in NL Central, third wild card)
Run differential: 35
Postseason: Lost to Los Angeles Dodgers 2-0 in NLWCS
The Reds had a respectable run differential but little star power aside from Elly De La Cruz and the often-injured Hunter Greene. Cincinnati beat out the Mets on a tiebreaker for the NL’s final postseason spot — seven games behind the No. 2 wild card — and then made a quick exit. The Reds’ best month was 15-11 and their worst was 12-15. Simply avoiding any extended slumps was enough to make the playoffs.

item.title: [bosoxinjection.com] Red Sox's Chad Tracy decision laid bare a 2027 managerial market reality
item.dc:creator: Brandon Glick
item.description: Rather than forcing fans to sit through a tense postseason run with an interim manager, the Boston Red Sox ripped the band-aid off and made one of the most obvious announcements of the season: Chad Tracy has earned the full-time manager job. item.content:encoded:
Rather than forcing fans to sit through a tense postseason run with an interim manager, the Boston Red Sox ripped the band-aid off and made one of the most obvious announcements of the season: Chad Tracy has earned the full-time manager job. The team and coach have agreed to a three-year extension that runs through 2029 with an option for the 2030 campaign.
It's a well-earned title, one which should take some pressure off Tracy ahead of his first foray into the postseason. Yet, as great as he's been, it's hard not to shake the feeling that this decision was as much about him as it was the coaching market.
By no means am I suggesting Tracy earned this job by default; this team was 32-46 just three months ago and then clinched a playoff spot with one week left to go in the regular season. Guiding the Red Sox out of that dark place into immediate success (they went 32-5 over their next 37 games) was nothing short of miraculous.
Rather, the point I'm trying to make is that Tracy was the only reasonable option for the Red Sox to go with. Just take a look at the best managerial candidates that are out there — none of them fit what this team needs moving forward.
Red Sox should be thankful Chad Tracy left them with no other choice for manager job
The clear-cut best option is Alex Cora, but considering Craig Breslow was also effectively extended (he had two years worth of options exercised), he was never returning to Boston. The odds are quite strong that he'll head to Philadelphia to take over for Don Mattingly, which means that competition for the other best candidates will be fierce this offseason.
Those include some retread hires like old friends David Ross and Rocco Baldelli, plus old enemy Brandon Hyde. The latter two in that group won Manager of the Year awards at their previous stops, but none of the trio are particularly inspiring. Baldelli is the only one with a record better than .500 as a skipper, and they've all combined for one playoff series win in 18 years.
Then there's the coaches looking for their first manager gig, including the likes of Carlos Beltrán and Albert Pujols. As exciting as it would have been to hire a Hall of Famer, moving on from Tracy just to hire another first-timer would have been a nonstarter. The biggest hole in his résumé is his lack of experience at the MLB level.
He's picked up some valuable experience this year, though, and the Red Sox are clearly better for it. Maybe this conversation would have been different if they never recovered from their first-half slump, but it's become clear over the past few months that Tracy really is the only man for the job.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Hope for Ceddanne Rafaela, Red Sox After Scary Exit

item.content:encoded:
It was a roller coaster of a day on Wednesday for the Boston Red Sox.
Early on in the day, the Red Sox activated outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela to make his first appearance for the club since Sep. 2. Rafaela was dealing with a quad injury that knocked him out of action for 17 games. With the playoffs right around the corner, the timing was perfect because it gave Boston's All-Star center fielder a few days to get right ahead of the postseason. But then things took a turn for the worse as Rafaela was forced to leave in the third inning of Wednesday's contest against the Cleveland Guardians due to what the club called right hamstring tightness.
With Rafaela out of the game, that certainly had the alarm bells ringing among Red Sox fans. But he gave the fanbase some hope after the game and shared that the injury felt "not even close" to as bad as his quad injury and that he thought it was just a cramp.
Ceddanne Rafaela Left Early On Wednesday
"On the swing, felt a little bit of a cramp," Rafaela said. "I was not happy in that moment ... Hopefully it's something that's just today or maybe tomorrow and go from there. ... Not even close [to as severe as the quad injury]. I think it was just a cramp. Maybe, not hydrated enough ... right now, it feels much better."
The plan is for the Red Sox center fielder to undergo an MRI on Thursday to test the severity of the hamstring injury to see if it is anything more than a cramp.
For the Red Sox's sake, the best-case scenario would be the injury simply being a cramp. There was a lot of excitement and it was his first game back after a few weeks off. It's easy to get caught up in a moment like that. If it was just a cramp, then that's something he likely could come back from on Thursday or even Friday. Boston has four games left in the regular season and ideally Rafaela will be in as many of them as possible.
The worst-case scenario would be the MRI revealing some sort of strain, or something of that nature, and Rafaela needing to miss even more time. The playoffs will begin in five days, as of writing, on Sep. 29. There isn't much wiggle room any longer when it comes to injuries. On Sep. 29, the Red Sox will begin a three-game Wild Card series. All it will take is two wins to advance to the American League Division Series at that point. Boston needs Rafaela to be at its best. Fortunately, he said he thought it was just a cramp. But now we wait.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [risingapple.com] The 25 greatest individual seasons in New York Mets history
item.dc:creator: Tim Boyle
item.description: Greatest is something every player who wears a New York Mets uniform strives for. Many come and go and are either forgotten about entirely or stick somewhere in the franchise’s lore for having one amazing moment. Fans know Mike Baxter for saving Johan Santana’s no-hitter. item.content:encoded:
Greatest is something every player who wears a New York Mets uniform strives for. Many come and go and are either forgotten about entirely or stick somewhere in the franchise’s lore for having one amazing moment. Fans know Mike Baxter for saving Johan Santana’s no-hitter. They’ll recall the name Mackey Sasser for the inability to throw the ball back to the pitcher safely. Kirk Nieuwenhuis had his random 3-home run game. Luis Castillo lives on in infamy for dropping a routine pop up at Yankee Stadium to end the night.
A mix of greatness and defeat have followed the Mets since they were officially born for the 1962 MLB season. Several Hall of Famers have come through to call the Polo Grounds, Shea Stadium, and Citi Field home. Everything from a mix of the homegrown talent of Tom Seaver to the ill-fated signing of Justin Verlander have a part in Mets history.
While some players live on forever with statues or their numbers retired, so do individual seasons. Random, expected, and in other seasons a longtime coming, these 25 individual seasons by Mets players are the greatest in the franchise’s history. You can’t think of these players without recalling how impressive of a year they had.
The 25 best seasons by Mets players in franchise history
25) Gary Carter, 1985
Gary Carter’s entrance into Mets lore began with a bang. Literally. He homered on Opening Day 1985 and would continue to pummel baseballs throughout the season for his new ball club. Carter finished with a 6.9 bWAR (what does that mean in 1985?) plus 32 home runs and 100 RBI. Exactly matching the .853 OPS he had in his final year with the Montreal Expos the year prior, it was the early telltale sign the Mets made the right decision to make him a part of their core. Partly because the Mets made the playoffs the next year, Carter was able to jump from sixth to third in the MVP vote. Despite this, his 1985 season was the better one.
24) Cleon Jones, 1969
Offense isn’t what won the Mets the 1969 World Series. The hitting was okay, but for the longest time, Cleon Jones’ .340 batting average sat well above anyone else in franchise history. Worth 7 bWAR in part because of an atypical season where he actually rated positively as a defender, Jones had an often-overlooked year where he finished 7th in the NL MVP vote. In an era when pitching dominated, Jones’ season deserves more credit. The year might not compare as well as some Mets years with 30+ home runs or 100+. However, for the timing of when it took place and the well-aged batting average, Jones deserves the accolades.
23) Jesse Orosco, 1983
Spoiler alert! There won’t be another relief pitcher on this list. They’re sometimes hard to judge because of how many fewer innings they throw. Plus, with the ever-evolving usage of arms, they don’t stack up well against each other in different eras. Nevertheless, what Jesse Orosco accomplished in 1983 was outlandish. At 13-7 all out of the bullpen, he tossed 110 innings and had a 1.47 ERA. The effort earned him third place in the NL Cy Young. It was a one-of-a-kind type of season from a Mets reliever. Somewhat unspoken, it was only his second full season as a major league pitcher and already he was at the top of his game while helping to further define the closer role.
22) Jose Reyes, 2006
Several different Jose Reyes seasons deserve to be on this list. How does one differentiate between them? He won a batting title in 2011 but lacked in other areas. In 2006, he hit .300, had a career-best 5.9 bWAR, and stole 64 bases. Most memorable was scoring 122 runs and driving in another 81. Homering 19 times helped make this maybe his most prolific offensive season for New York. The 2006 Mets are remembered for their incredible lineup. Reyes at the very top was one of the biggest factors.
21) Edgardo Alfonzo, 2000
Edgardo Alfonzo is a beloved Mets player. He crosses off a lot of the boxes fans desire. He was homegrown, versatile, and put together some really good years for winning ball clubs. In 2000, he wasn’t the main attraction and yet the season’s totals hold up nicely all of these years later. His lone All-Star season included a career-best 6.4 bWAR with 25 home runs and 94 RBI. Both of those numbers were a little short of what he did the year previous. However, his .967 OPS overpowered any of his past seasons and remains one of the best in Mets history. Alfonzo could be trusted to hit anywhere from first to fifth in the lineup if needed.
20) Lance Johnson, 1996
The 1996 Mets weren’t very good, but they did have three players who hit really well. One of the trio put together a season that landed him on the record books and doesn’t look like it’ll be surpassed. Lance Johnson’s 227 hits and 21 triples both set single-season Mets records while leading the league. In addition to the bat, he stole 50 bases and earned himself a 1.9 dWAR. If we were ranking only seasons by Mets leadoff hitters, this would be right near the top. It’s a shame this couldn’t have occurred on a better season for the team.
19) Jerry Koosman, 1968
Jerry Koosman did something amazing. By many measurements, his best year was his first. Koosman had a small sampling in the majors during the 1967 season. The following year qualified as his rookie campaign. Koosman went 19-12 with a 2.08 ERA. He’d end up 13th in the Cy Young race and the runner-up for the Rookie of the Year, just barely, when Johnny Bench beat him for the honor. A coin toss might have been the decider for some voters as both NL rookies had a case. Koosman was later the Cy Young runner-up in 1976. Compared to 1968, his freshman year was the better of the two.
18) David Cone, 1988
Who says wins don’t matter? In 1988, David Cone went a remarkable 20-3. He wasn’t vulturing wins thanks to the help of a strong offense. Cone pitched to a 2.22 ERA while finishing third in the Cy Young race and 10th in the MVP vote. A somewhat underrated pitcher whose career spanned the lighter hitting 1980s through the Steroid Era of the 1990s, this first full season in a Mets uniform was a preview of the strikeout machine he’d later become. Fanning 212, he’d later manage to lead the league in 1990 and 1991. The ERA in 1988 was about a full run better making this the more worthy campaign.
17) Pete Alonso, 2019
Pete Alonso posted some of the most unique statistics in Mets history. The power is unmatched in a single season and career. His rookie season in 2019 featuring 53 home runs and 120 RBI also included a 5.4 bWAR and a career-high .941 OPS. The record-setting debut season out of Alonso was more than enough to make a lasting impression on Mets fans who will never stop loving him. Alonso, like some others on this list, gets bonus points for doing it as a rookie. Those 53 home runs will be tough for a veteran, let alone a player with no MLB experience, to ever match. He became the Mets home run king for a reason. His power is unmatched from just the eye test.
16) Juan Soto, 2025
Statistically impressive, the only thing missing from Juan Soto’s first year with the Mets was purpose. The team collapsed late despite Soto putting together yet another one of his token MVP-caliber seasons. Along with hitting 43 home runs and posting a league-high .396 OBP, Soto stole 38 bases. His previous single-season high was 12. Truly a one-of-a-kind type of year, the only reason this isn’t higher is because the defense slowed him down. It was the type of year to build off of while making his record-setting contract worth it to Steve Cohen.
15) Francisco Lindor, 2024
Francisco Lindor’s MVP runner-up season in 2024 needs to be experienced to fully understand. He started off as poorly as the team and managed to quite literally lead the club to the NLCS. His first 30/30 season which includes his time in Cleveland was far more complicated than just looking at the .844 OPS. Lindor was a leader and with another Gold Glove-caliber season at shortstop, managed to put together a 6.8 bWAR season. Nothing about the season was statistically insane yet Lindor seemed to do a little bit of everything well.
14) Darryl Strawberry, 1987
Strangely, the best season of Darryl Strawberry’s career with the Mets took place in a non-playoff campaign. The 1987 Mets were good, but not good enough. Strawberry set new career highs with 39 home runs and 104 RBI. Slashing .284/.398/.583 with 36 stolen bases, it was maybe the most complete year Strawberry had as an offensive player. Although he’d lead the league in multiple offensive categories in 1988, many of his 1987 totals were superior. Crossing 30 home runs and 100 RBI for the first time in his career, it was a bit of a transition from Strawberry being one of the star players to be the signature member of the Mets.
13) Bernard Gilkey, 1996
Mets fans who weren’t familiar with Bernard Gilkey’s work might assume he was always one of the better middle of the order hitters. Arriving via trade with the St. Louis Cardinals prior to the 1996 season, Gilkey cranked it up to a whole new level. It feels appropriate that he’d later make a cameo in Men in Black because Gilkey’s numbers were unworldly. He slashed .317/.393/.562 with 44 doubles, 30 home runs, and 117 RBI. The doubles are still the most of any Mets player in a single-season. The 8.1 bWAR became the best in Mets history by a position player. Created by both his bat and glove, Gilkey led the league with 18 assists, 4 double plays, 309 putouts, and ranked as the best at his position in range factor.
12) Tom Seaver, 1975
You knew Tom Seaver was coming eventually. His 1975 season earned him his third and final Cy Young Award. He probably could have had more. This season was a 7.8 bWAR campaign that had him going 22-9 with a 2.38 ERA and a league-leading 243 strikeouts. Compared to most players, it’s incredible. On the list of Seaver performances, this one is easy to overlook because even one of his non-Cy Young winning years was better. Don’t worry. Tom Terrific is all over this list with several seasons that were even better.
11) Tom Seaver, 1969
When it comes to Mets greatness, Tom Seaver is the “you haven’t seen the last of me!” in franchise history. The 1969 season ended with a championship for the Mets. In the regular season, Seaver won a franchise-record 25 games while on his way to his first Cy Young and an MVP runner-up. Neither the 2.21 ERA nor 208 strikeouts would set personal bests. This might have been the most rewarding individual season of Seaver’s career yet it falls short of his best by quite a couple. At least he got winning the big one out of the way relatively early.
10) Jacob deGrom, 2019
Speaking of Cy Young Mets seasons, Jacob deGrom got his second in 2019. His 7.2 bWAR led the league as did the 255 strikeouts. By this point, greatness was something Mets fans weren’t demanding from deGrom, it was expected. A good length away from some of those other memorable Mets seasons by pitchers like Tom Seaver, his 2.43 ERA doesn’t even do him justice for how dominant he was for his second straight season as the best pitcher in the sport. Sadly, this would end up as his final full season in a Mets uniform due to a pandemic as well as injuries in 2021 and 2022.
9) Mike Piazza, 2000
Mike Piazza had big years, moments, and numbers with the Mets. Because his defense behind the plate was never good, stats like WAR don’t rank quite as high as some others. The 2000 season was big regardless as Piazza hit .324/.398/.614 with a 1.012 OPS. The OPS was the largest in any full season for a Mets player. The year included 38 home runs and 113 RBI with the real kicker being that he had only 482 at-bats. One of those more underrated qualities about his offensive abilities, he walked 58 times while only going down on strikes 69 times.
8) Howard Johnson, 1989
Howard Johnson led the league in home runs and RBI in 1991, but it was his 1989 season which deserves a spot on this list. Armed with 36 home runs and 101 RBI, Johnson’s speed went on display with 41 stolen bases. It was his second 30/30 season with the Mets. He hit .287 as well, atypical for the .251 he hit while in orange and blue. Never the biggest star on the Mets roster during his best years in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Johnson’s powerful and speedy 1989 campaign was a special one and the best representation of what he had to offer the ball club during his peak seasons.
7) John Olerud, 1998
Each of the three seasons John Olerud spent with the Mets was special in its own way. A franchise-leading .354 batting average helps break the tie. That’s what he hit in 1998, his middle season with the club. Posting a 7.6 bWAR as well, Olerud was the 12th place finisher in the MVP race during a season where you didn’t get much attention if you weren’t hitting home runs. He had 22 with 93 RBI. More like Keith Hernandez leveled up on offense, newer statistics that emphasis on base have helped this season age better. Olerud was never the best first baseman in the league. In Mets history, he’s right there as one of the stronger overall performers.
6) Carlos Beltran, 2006
Carlos Beltran overcame a rough first year with the Mets in 2005 to put together one of the all-time great ones in 2006. The 41 home runs hit by Todd Hundley in 1996 were matched by Beltran. Posting an 8.2 bWAR, he set a new single-season high in franchise history that would only get to enjoy one season at the top. Beltran slashed .275/.388/.594. He had 95 walks and only 99 strikeouts to practically cancel each other out. The only negative about his season was how it ended. The visual of striking out looking to end Game 7 of the NLCS remains one of the first fans often think about when his name or heartbreaking Mets moments are mentioned.
5) David Wright, 2007
No Mets player has ever matched the popularity of David Wright. His 2007 season, an 8.3 bWAR campaign, set a new mark of excellence. This was Captain America at his absolute best. He hit 30 home runs, stole 34 bases, and cruised past 100 runs scored and RBI. He even hit .325 with a .416 OBP. To make sure no check boxes were left unfilled, he won a Silver Slugger and Gold Glove. The team’s collapse in 2007 likely had to do a lot with why he only finished fourth in the MVP.
4) Jacob deGrom, 2018
As much as Jacob deGrom’s ridiculously good 15-start season in 2021 was historic, it wasn’t a complete year. The 2018 season, on the other hand, included 32 starts and a magnificent 1.70 ERA. This was deGrom’s true coming out party. The debate all year was whether or not a pitcher with a losing record could win the Cy Young. He finished at 10-9 to void the conversation and was one vote shy of a unanimous decision for his first time winning the award. The season included multiple highs for deGrom including 269 strikeouts. It was the ultimate one-man army type of season in Mets history where the team was, oftentimes, only worth watching every fifth day.
3) Tom Seaver, 1971
Here’s the most ridiculous detail about the 1971 season for Tom Seaver: he didn’t win the Cy Young. A league-leading 10.2 bWAR wouldn’t have been known at the time, but a 20-10 record and league-best 1.76 ERA as well as 289 strikeouts to overtake every other pitcher in the National League should have been enough. Seaver settled as the runner-up to Ferguson Jenkins who had a 2.77 ERA and a 24-13 record. The race wasn’t even all that close with Jenkins getting 17 first-place votes and Seaver receiving 6. Both the Mets and Chicago Cubs won 83 games so it’s not as if team record mattered at all. In practically any other year, Seaver would have added more hardware to his collection.
2) Tom Seaver, 1973
If you crave Tom Seaver content, you’re in the right place. His 1973 season earned him his second Cy Young. He had a career-best 10.6 bWAR featuring a league-high 2.08 ERA, 18 complete games, and 251 strikeouts. The Mets would sneak into the postseason and then overtake the Big Red Machine Cincinnati Reds on their way to the World Series. The Mets fell short, of course, but the regular season showing by Seaver was valuable at cementing his Hall of Fame legacy. We can even include the playoffs if there was any doubt. Although he was 1-2 overall, he pitched to a 1.62 ERA in the NLCS and had a 2.40 ERA in the World Series. All the Mets were missing was league-average offense to win another championship.
1) Dwight Gooden, 1985
There shouldn’t have been any question as to what the best season by a Mets player was going to be because what Dwight Gooden did in 1985 was one of the greatest in MLB history. The 12.2 bWAR ranks as the 26th best in MLB history. It’s the best after 1913. Gooden went 24-4 with a 1.53 ERA. He led the league in complete games, innings, and struck out 268 batters. Those numbers matter a lot, as does one other one. Gooden was only 20-years-old for the entire season. This is the kind of year that’ll go unmatched by a Mets player until some sort of cosmic shift in the way the game is played or with the rule book. You can safely etch this into stone as the best.
Hall of Famers, players with retired numbers, some completely random yet memorable performances, and even a few active members cracked the list of the best individual Mets player seasons. Records were broken. Memories were made. In a couple of cases, championships were won.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Pedro Martinez on Game 7 in 2003, no regrets on calling the Yankees his daddy, and a mission to help - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Dan Shaughnessy
item.description: Many of us believe he’s the best pitcher we’ve ever seen. He’s a blue-chip, first-ballot Hall of Famer, part of the Red Sox team that broke the Curse, and seen on TBS after Sox playoff games in any given October. He’ll be 55 next month and spends every year shuttling between Boston and his native Dominican Republic, when he’s not working in Atlanta.
