item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox kept outfielder Jarren Duran out of the starting lineup again Wednesday night as they hosted the Cleveland Guardians in the second game of a three-game series at Fenway Park.
Manager Chad Tracy’s posted batting order featured Roman Anthony in left field, Nick Sogard at first base, Jahmai Jones as the designated hitter, Wilyer Abreu in right field, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Ceddanne Rafaela in center field, Caleb Durbin at third base, Trevor Story at shortstop and Andruw Monasterio at second base. Sonny Gray was listed as the starting pitcher.
Duran also sat Tuesday, when the Guardians beat the Red Sox 3-2. He entered that game as a pinch-hitter and drew a walk.
Cleveland took the series opener on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly in the ninth inning. The Guardians stranded 15 runners but still extended their winning streak to six games.
Boston dropped to 84-73. The club already clinched an American League Wild Card berth Sunday but has lost three straight and eight of its last 12.
Duran entered Wednesday batting .204 with 110 hits, 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, 65 runs and 19 stolen bases in 146 games. He had 538 at-bats, 39 walks and 163 strikeouts.
The left-handed hitter has struggled in September. He was 9-for-50 with one home run and one RBI in 17 games this month before Tuesday’s appearance.
Over his last 15 games he was 8-for-42 with one homer. His on-base-plus-slugging percentage sat at .625 for the season.
Rafaela’s return to center field tightened the outfield picture. Anthony has been starting in left and Abreu in right, leaving Duran as the extra outfielder in many recent games.
Tracy had the interim tag removed Tuesday and was named the franchise’s 49th manager. The Red Sox have used a mix of platoons and rest days for Duran down the stretch.
Gray brings a 17-5 record and 2.82 ERA into the start. Cleveland is expected to counter with Forrest Griffin.
The Guardians sit at 82-75 and hold a one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox in the AL Central. Chicago owns the season-series tiebreaker.
Duran, 30, is in his sixth major league season, all with Boston. He was an All-Star in 2024.
He still ranks among the team leaders in home runs and RBIs despite the low batting average. His 20 homers leave him one short of his career high.
The Red Sox close the regular season with this series, then host the Chicago Cubs for three games. Seeding and rest for the Wild Card round remain in play.
Duran’s speed and defense have kept him in the mix even as his batting average dropped. He stole 19 bases and continued to play a plus outfield when used.
Boston’s offense produced eight hits Tuesday. Rutschman went 3-for-4 and pinch-hitter Mickey Gasper tied the game with a home run in the eighth.
Cleveland collected 12 hits. Angel Martínez finished 3-for-4.
The Red Sox sit 12 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East. The Yankees hold the other Wild Card spot six games ahead of Boston.
Duran’s role for the final week and any postseason series will depend on how Tracy balances the four outfielders available.

Boston Red Sox Make Intriguing Jarren Duran Decision

Duran remains out of the lineup on Wednesday.

The former All-Star is in the middle of his 6th MLB season (all with the Red Sox).
Looking At The Red Sox Right Now
The Red Sox are the third-place team in the American League East with an 84-73 record in 157 games.
They have lost six out of their last ten games (and are 38-38 in 76 games at home).
Talkin’ Yanks wrote (on Tuesday): “Yankees have clinched a higher seed than the Red Sox, which means they will host Boston in the three-game Wild Card series in the likely event that the two teams meet in the postseason next Tuesday through Thursday”
Following two more games with the Guardians, the Red Sox will finish the regular season against the Chicago Cubs (at home).
ESPN’s Buster Olney wrote: “The current thinking among the powers that be is that the Cubs and Red Sox will play a doubleheader Friday, and then an afternoon game Saturday.”
Looking At The Guardians
The Guardians are the top team in the American League Central with an 82-75 record in 157 games.
They are just 1.0 game ahead of the Chicago White Sox (who are in second).
Following the Red Sox, the Guardians will finish the 2026 regular season when they visit the Kansas City Royals.

item.title: [blogs.fangraphs.com] The Weakest Positions on the Remaining American League Contenders
item.dc:creator: Jay Jaffe

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees had to make do without Aaron Judge for all of June, July and August due to a stress fracture in his right first rib. With the days on the calendar dwindling and the AL East title still in play — which is no longer the case after the Rays clinched on Tuesday night — Judge bypassed a rehab assignment, but once he returned, he played in just seven games before landing back on the injured list due to a right calf strain. Both the slugger and the team took great pains to avoid discussing the injury’s specificity and timeline for recovery until Tuesday, when manager Aaron Boone revealed that Judge has a “moderate grade” strain, received a platelet-poor plasma injection, and isn’t expected to be available for the team’s Wild Card Series rematch against the Red Sox.
While deadline acquisition Heliot Ramos has heated up after a very slow start to his pinstriped career, the Yankees’ right field situation is one of the more glaring potential trouble spots among American League contenders. As the playoffs approach, teams no longer have a chance to upgrade from outside their organizations and instead must make do with the talent on hand. What follows here is a look at the most vulnerable teams at each position — something of a companion to my annual pre-deadline Replacement Level Killers series, with a focus on the teams that still have a chance to make the playoffs. For the AL, that means the Rays, Yankees, and Red Sox — all of whom have clinched spots — plus the Guardians, White Sox, Rangers, and Astros, who are battling for the other two division titles and the third Wild Card spot. I’ve taken the Blue Jays out of consideration, as their Playoff Odds now start with a zero in front of the decimal. While full-season performances play a significant part here, I’m more concerned with who’s worst now, with injuries and adjustments in mind. Each position has a headliner (or two, if it’s a job share), but at several positions, I’ve noted other teams with concerns. A companion National League piece will follow.
Catcher: Kyle Teel and Jake Rogers, White Sox
A Top 100 prospect in both 2024 and ’25, Kyle Teel did a very solid job as a rookie last season, hitting for a 125 wRC+ with 1.9 WAR in just 78 games, but he missed the first two months of this season due to a Grade 2 right hamstring strain and then an LCL sprain in his right knee. His replacements, mainly Edgar Quero (a three-time Top 100 prospect) and Drew Romo, struggled so mightily that they headed the catchers’ section on my Replacement Level Killers list, with Quero optioned to Triple-A Charlotte once Teel returned. While Teel’s defense has been an upgrade, he’s hit just .178/.302/.318 (81 wRC+) with an astronomical 37.3% strikeout rate, up from last year’s 25.9%, and his average exit velocity is just 84.5 mph, down from last year’s 88.3 mph. He recently missed time with a left ankle sprain as well.
Romo was optioned to Charlotte in early September during a shuffle that included both Teel’s return and the arrival of the 31-year-old Jake Rogers via the waiver wire. Rogers, who began the year with the Tigers, was traded to the Orioles in late July, then flipped to the Red Sox in the Adley Rutschman trade on August 3 before being sent on his merry way again within a fortnight. He’s now playing for his fourth team this season and has hit just .161/.276/.287 (62 wRC+). All told, White Sox catchers have combined for a 54 wRC+ and -0.4 WAR, both of which rank 29th in the majors; for as much long-term potential as the 24-year-old Teel and 23-year-old Quero (who has played sparingly since being recalled) may have, they’re less than ideal right now.
It’s worth noting that Rutschman, who was on the injured list due to left wrist inflammation when he was sent to Boston as part of a seven-player blockbuster, has struggled to the point that he’s a concern as well. The 28-year-old switch-hitter was batting a solid .251/.331/.433 (116 wRC+) before being sidelined for three weeks — his third IL stint this season, with shorter ones for left ankle inflammation and a concussion while with Baltimore — but he’s hit just .214/.270/.398 (82 wRC+) in 111 plate appearances since being activated. His strikeout rate has spiked from 14.1% to 21.6%, and his average exit velo has fallen by about two ticks. Backup Connor Wong has hit a similarly light .234/.310/.346 (84 wRC+), albeit with dreadful defense (-10 FRV, -8 DRS, -6.6 FRM). The good news is that Rutschman went 3-for-4 with a pair of doubles on Tuesday night against the Guardians; the bad news is that the Red Sox have other injury concerns in their lineup as well.
First Base: Nathaniel Lowe and David Fry, Guardians
Guardians first basemen made my Killers list due to the light production of their platoon of Kyle Manzardo and Rhys Hoskins. At the deadline, they dealt for Nathaniel Lowe and optioned Manzardo to Triple-A Columbus. A couple of week later, they placed Hoskins on the IL due to lower back inflammation and turned to David Fry, a utilityman who can catch. Alas, after getting a 94 wRC+ from their first basemen prior to the deadline, they’ve managed just a 90 wRC+ since. The lefty-swinging Lowe, who hit a robust .266/.341/.480 (123 wRC+) for the Reds, has dipped to .228/.279/.390 (83 wRC+) while hitting a ton of popups. The righty-swinging Fry has done well in his limited duty at first base, but has hit just .192/.312/.349 (90 wRC+) in 202 plate appearances overall.
Hoskins began a swing progression nearly two weeks ago, but with Columbus’ season having ended, a rehab assignment isn’t an option, which doesn’t bode well for an uptick from his .179/.306/.376 (95 wRC+) line. Manzardo (.215/.306/.378, 95 wRC+) didn’t hit the ball as hard at Columbus as he had either in his previous stops there or in Cleveland, and there hasn’t been any buzz about bringing him back in September or October.
Meanwhile in Boston, Willson Contreras has been the team’s top hitter, batting a potent .276/.387/.518 (152 wRC+) with 27 homers, but he’s been limited to four games this month between a left hamstring strain and a hit-by-pitch induced bruised knuckle on his right hand. Fortunately, he avoided a fracture, and returned to swinging a bat on September 20; the Red Sox hope to get him into the lineup before the end of the regular season, but the situation bears monitoring. Mickey Gasper and Nick Sogard have shared duties during his absence. Both have provided above-average production overall; Gasper had been in a 4-for-32 slump before hitting a pinch-homer — his 10th long ball in 218 plate appearances — against the Guardians on Tuesday night.
Second Base: Jose Altuve, Astros
Jose Altuve may wind up in Cooperstown some day, but Father Time has caught up to the diminutive 36-year-old. He’s batting just .250/.308/.402, which has taken a bite out of both the Astros’ offense and his chances at reaching 3,000 hits; his 99 wRC+ is his lowest full-season mark since 2013, while his .327 xSLG is a 57-point drop from last season and a Statcast-era low. What’s more, his defense has reached its nadir, with both his -10 FRV and -16 DRS rating not only as career worsts but also major league worsts at his position. With Yordan Alvarez entrenched at designated hitter and too valuable to risk in left field — he hasn’t used his glove in a postseason game since 2023 — there’s no place to hide Altuve, but also little likelihood he’ll be benched in favor of backup Nick Allen (.271/.318/.371, 95 wRC+).
On the injury front, keep an eye on the return of the Yankees’ Jazz Chisholm Jr., who was activated between games of Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Rays after missing 12 games due to a sprained right thumb. While his offense has dipped from a 125 wRC+ last year to 100 (.233/.313/.403) this year, Chisholm’s 3.4 WAR ranks third among the team’s position players behind Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger, and his total of 19 home runs ranks second. Backups Anthony Volpe (.244/.321/.335, 88 wRC+) and José Caballero (.236/.293/.373, 86 wRC+) are substantial steps down, but if Chisholm has any lingering issues, one of them may be needed to fill in.
Third Base: Ryan McMahon and Amed Rosario, Yankees
Yankees third basemen have combined for -0.1 WAR, the majors’ third-lowest mark. Lefty-swinging Ryan McMahon bears the bulk of the responsibility for that, hitting just .206/.274/.341 (73 wRC+) while playing solid defense. Righty-swinging Amed Rosario has produced a 100 wRC+ while playing third but has hit just .233/.275/.406 (87 wRC+) overall, and he’s been lousy at the hot corner, with -6 DRS and -6 FRV in just 309.1 innings. The righty-swinging Caballero is at least a better defender than Rosario and about on par offensively, and he’s one of the league’s top base thieves, with 34 steals in 45 attempts. He has also out-produced Rosario against lefties, with an 81 wRC+ to Rosario’s 63 — which could be a factor given that the Red Sox can call upon lefties Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle to start during the Wild Card Series.
Shortstop: Taylor Walls, Rays
For the third year in a row, the defensive metrics have been very split with regards to Taylor Walls. His 21 DRS leads all shortstops (nobody else has more than 10 DRS), but his -2 FRV ranks 23rd out of 30 with at least 500 innings at the position. Between the latter mark and his dismal .222/.308/.294 (73 wRC+) line, he’s produced just 0.7 WAR. That said, neither Jorge Mateo (.205/.250/.318, 55 wRC+) nor Ben Williamson (.244/.304/.327, 79 wRC+), his occasional fill-ins, hits well enough to merit surpassing Wells on the depth chart.
Left Field: Taylor Trammell and LaMonte Wade Jr., Astros
The Astros’ current 1.3 WAR from their left fielders ranks 17th in the majors, ahead of both the Guardians (1.2) and Red Sox (0.8). But between Steven Kwan’s second-half heater and Roman Anthony’s return from a torn tendon in his right ring finger, both of those teams are now in a better spot than Houston. Taylor Trammell made several Top 100 lists as a prospect — he was as high as no. 12 as a 60-FV on our 2019 list — but he’s now 29 and has netted 0.1 WAR in 273 major league games for four different teams. This year he’s hit .200/.292/.355 (84 wRC+) in a career-high 95 games spread across the three outfield positions, with a 95 wRC+ in 237 plate appearances against righties and a 19 wRC+ (ouch) in 41 plate appearances against lefties.
LaMonte Wade Jr., a reliable contributor for the Giants from 2021–24, bottomed out to a 53 wRC+ last year in a season split between San Francisco and Anaheim. He spent the first few months of this season in the White Sox organization but was released on June 1 so he could sign with the Astros, for whom he’s hit .208/.308/.352 (90 wRC+). He’s been protected from facing many lefties and has seen his playing time dry up otherwise, as he’s been in a slump since mid-August. Meanwhile, righty-swinging Nelson Velázquez hasn’t made a very strong case for himself by hitting .192/.255/.414 (81 wRC+) with a 33.6% strikeout rate in 110 plate appearances split between the Cardinals and Astros. With options like these, you can see why playing Alvarez in left and DHing Altuve starts to make some sense.
Center Field: Daulton Varsho, Astros
The first-half struggles of Jake Meyers, Brice Matthews and Trammell landed the Astros on the Killers center field list, so they quite reasonably dealt for Daulton Varsho on August 3. The 30-year-old flychaser was hitting .243/.307/.375 (91 wRC+), and while his once-elite defense has regressed towards average, a performance like that is still good enough to carry the position. He looked like a decent upgrade for Houston, but while his defense has remained solid enough, he’s hit an anemic .172/.224/.311 (48 wRC+), with his strikeout and walk rates both moving in the wrong direction.
A closer look shows that Varsho has actually been hitting the ball slightly harder since the trade, but all season, he’s been producing popups and cans of corn galore because he’s getting under so many pitches. The real fall-off is relative to last year; his pulled air rate has fallen from 29.5% to 18.5%, while his xSLG has dropped from .464 to .354. As with Altuve and the left field situation, the Astros don’t have great alternatives. Matthews, a 24-year-old rookie, has hit just .201/.255/.332 (64 wRC+), and Meyers sustained a season-ending left kneecap injury at Triple-A Sugar Land last week.
Yet another injury-related note for the Red Sox: Ceddanne Rafaela was sidelined nearly three weeks ago due to a right quad strain. Prior to that, he was putting the finishing touches on a breakout season, having hit .282/.317/.443 (108 wRC+) with 16 homers and 17 steals while playing Gold Glove-caliber defense in center field. Less than a week after he went down, his capable fill-in Eli White suffered a ligament injury in his right foot, requiring season-ending surgery. Since then, Jarren Duran and Nate Eaton have shared the position. Rafaela has yet to return to the roster, though manager Chad Tracy said he’s “getting close.” If he does suffer a setback, continuing to play Duran during what’s been an awful season (.204/.261/.362, 68 wRC+) would obviously be less than ideal.
The Yankees’ Trent Grisham was sidelined by a Grade 2 strain of his right hamstring around the same time that Rafaela went down, and he has yet to return as well. His performance has fallen off drastically after a career year; he’s hit just .211/.308/.395 (98 wRC+) with 18 homers while trading some power for contact, and his defense has also been rough (-5 FRV and -8 DRS in 961.1 innings). While Boone has said he could be “in play at some point” during the postseason, there’s little urgency. Rookie Spencer Jones has shifted over from right field and done an impressive job of holding down the fort, playing adequate defense while hitting .246/.316/.435 (110 wRC+) despite a 36.2% strikeout rate.
Right Field: Heliot Ramos and Aaron Judge, Yankees
Yes, that looks weird in print, but for the moment at least, it’s a reality for the Yankees. The 27-year-old Ramos hit a modest .264/.304/.424 (100 wRC+) with nine homers and 0.6 WAR for the Giants before being traded to the Yankees on August 3. He began his time in pinstripes by going 5-for-47, and at one point went 32 games between homers — from July 20 to August 29 — while slugging .204. He’s heated up since then, but his .168/.294/.356 (85 wRC+) line with the Yankees doesn’t give anyone much confidence he can replace even the banged-up version of Judge the Yankees have received in his 66 games this season (.241/.360/.511, 141 wRC+).
In terms of concerns about sheer replacement-level production, the White Sox stand out here. Early in the season, the team tried Everson Pereira, Jarred Kelenic, and Rikuu Nishida as their regular at the position, but none got the job done. On June 9 they called up Braden Montgomery, a switch-hitting 23-year-old who placed 100th on our Top 100 as a 50-FV prospect in the spring. He collected two hits in his debut that night against the Braves, capped by a walk-off homer, but it’s been mostly downhill since then, as he’s hit .212/.305/.340 (84 wRC+) with six homers and 0.5 WAR in 88 games. While he’s hit .248/.344/.385 (110 wRC+) in 250 plate appearances against righties, he’s flailed away at a .125/.204/.2227 clip in 98 plate appearances against lefties. With resurgent lefty-masher Randal Grichuk on the roster and hitting .331/.372/.650 (182 wRC+) in 172 plate appearances against lefties, there’s no reason that should be happening.
Designated Hitter: Andrew Benintendi, White Sox
No remaining AL contender ranks below 15th in the majors in wRC+ provided by their DHs, and the two lowest teams from among that subset, the Red Sox and Guardians, are respectively third and fourth in second-half wRC+ from that spot while using revolving casts of players. So I’m picking (on) Andrew Benintendi, who has hit a very modest .243/.302/.414 (98 wRC+) while starting at DH in 105 games, with Grichuk (19) the only other Chicago player in double digits. There’s nothing particularly terrible or mysterious about Benintendi’s performance, which beyond a September slump, has lined up with his expected stats quite well; he’s got 21st-percentile bat speed but a 66th-percentile squared-up rate and a 77th-percentile hard-hit rate. He doesn’t hit lefties (.227/.261/.250, 44 wRC+ in 47 PA this year), so manager Will Venable has either used Grichuk or one of his righty regulars there. For as impressive as the White Sox’s turnaround from three straight 100-loss seasons has been, you can see from this roundup that the team’s weaknesses have come to the fore as they’ve tried to sew up a playoff berth.
Brooklyn-based Jay Jaffe is a senior writer for FanGraphs, the author of The Cooperstown Casebook (Thomas Dunne Books, 2017) and the creator of the JAWS (Jaffe WAR Score) metric for Hall of Fame analysis. He founded the Futility Infielder website (2001), was a columnist for Baseball Prospectus (2005-2012) and a contributing writer for Sports Illustrated (2012-2018). He has been a recurring guest on MLB Network and a member of the BBWAA since 2011, and a Hall of Fame voter since 2021. Follow him on BlueSky @jayjaffe.bsky.social.

item.content:encoded:
The plan for Alex Bregman to face his former team at Fenway Park just got scrapped. He will most likely miss the series against the Boston Red Sox after taking a foul ball to the face. This bad luck happened on Sunday during a game in Cincinnati, not Boston. The foul ball struck him while he stood in the on-deck circle warming up for his turn at bat.
The injury is worse than a simple bruise. Bregman suffered multiple facial fractures, according to ESPN's Jeff Passan. Michael Busch's bat launched the ball directly into the third baseman's cheek. A trainer accompanied him as he descended the dugout stairs, face buried in his hands. The Cubs sent him straight to the hospital after the game to get checked out.
No Surgery, But No Certainty
Doctors decided he will not undergo surgery to fix the breaks. Yet that choice does not mean the bones do not need attention. Bregman is hopeful to return in the playoffs, but the timeline looks shaky. According to reports, extensive damage may prevent him from recovering before the postseason.
Photos shared by the player show just how bad the hit was. An image revealed his face with a bloodied cheek and a black eye swollen shut. By the following morning, the left side of his face had become entirely swollen. Craig Counsell, the Chicago manager, stated Bregman suffered a hit to the left cheekbone below his eye, resulting in a bleeding nose.
Fenway Park Might Wait Too Long
The Red Sox series is a key moment for any fan who follows the sport. Seeing Bregman play against the team he once knew would have been a special story. Instead, the Cubs star faces a long road to recovery. Although no diagnosis exists yet, predicting a timely return for Bregman from this injury seems difficult.
The timing makes the loss of the Fenway series even more painful. His playoff spot is uncertain, and he will likely miss the series at Fenway Park. The team won the game 9-1 over the Reds, but the victory feels hollow without their star third baseman.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

23 Sep 2026, 18:49 GMT+10

(Photo credit: David Butler II)
The Boston Red Sox hope to shift some momentum in advance of the playoffs when they host the Cleveland Guardians on Wednesday night in the second game of a three-game series.
Cleveland extended its winning streak to six games by beating Boston 3-2 on Tuesday. It was the third straight loss for the Red Sox (84-73), who have dropped eight of their last 12 games and own a 9-10 record in September but still clinched a wild-card berth on Sunday.Add left-handed reliever Erik Miller to the list of Boston's concerns as the Red Sox prepare for the playoffs. Miller looked sharp when the Red Sox acquired him from San Francisco in August, but he has allowed nine walks and hit two batters in September.One of those hit batsmen scored the game-winning run Tuesday. Miller hit Chase DeLauter to start the ninth inning, and DeLauter ended up breaking a 2-2 tie when he scored on Nathaniel Lowe's sacrifice fly.Miller has given up six runs and six walks in his past 3 1/3 innings and took the loss on Tuesday.'He's working through stuff,' Boston manager Chad Tracy said. 'I thought today was another step in the right direction. The hit batter ... the free passes are what gets you, and I think he also got some bad batted ball (luck). ... We're gonna try to get him out there a couple more times this week. Obviously still trust the stuff. If we can get that right, trust the stuff and his ability to strike out guys.'
Tuesday's win allowed the Guardians (82-75) to remain one game ahead of the Chicago White Sox at the top of the American League Central standings. Chicago has the division tiebreaker over Cleveland, which has a magic number of two to clinch a playoff berth.
Meanwhile, Guardians manager Stephen Vogt called Lowe 'a professional hitter.'
'You know he's not trying to do too much,' Vogt said. 'He's not going up there trying to be a hero, hitting a three-run homer. Just score the guy from third. Got a pitch up in the zone, and was able to drive it deep enough to left. And you know he continues to just make plays for us.'The Guardians won despite stranding 15 runners and a 1-for-12 hitting performance with runners in scoring position.'Again, felt like it was another night where we get a ton of traffic, we put a lot of pressure on, and just weren't able to get the big hit,' Vogt said. 'You know, we were able to get a couple runs across, but we left a lot on the table. But I just love the way we're making guys work. We're getting on base ... and we're going to come through a lot more often than not. And again, our pitching just picked us up again tonight.'Tracy said he expects center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela (quadriceps) to be activated from the injured list on Wednesday. The manager also said first baseman Willson Contreras still has some soreness in his hand and won't be in the lineup Wednesday but is close to returning.Right-hander Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.82 ERA) will start for the Red Sox on Wednesday. He's 8-5 with a 3.12 ERA in 21 career starts against the Guardians. On May 30, he gave up one run on four hits and three walks over six innings against them. He struck out seven in a 9-1 win.Left-hander Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67 ERA) will start for Cleveland on Wednesday. It will be his first career appearance against the Red Sox.--Field Level Media

item.title: [dailycampus.com] Brayden’s Breakdown: Boston Red Sox postseason preview
item.dc:creator: Brayden Gorski
item.description: The Boston Red Sox clinched their second consecutive playoff berth Sunday and their third since 2021. It was a season with the highest of highs and the lowest of lows in Boston as they started the season 10-17 before firing longtime manager Alex Cora. In June, the Red Sox found themselves 14 games under .500 at a record of 32-46. This is when everything changed. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox clinched their second consecutive playoff berth Sunday and their third since 2021.
It was a season with the highest of highs and the lowest of lows in Boston as they started the season 10-17 before firing longtime manager Alex Cora.
In June, the Red Sox found themselves 14 games under .500 at a record of 32-46. This is when everything changed.
They swept the New York Yankees before losing two out of three games to the Washington Nationals.
The Red Sox went on the road and swept the Los Angeles Angels, Chicago White Sox and New York Mets to sit at 46-48 heading into the all-star break.
After nine straight road wins, the Red Sox headed home to face the 56-38 Tampa Bay Rays. Tampa has had Boston’s number in the past few seasons, but this weekend was different.
In the first game of a doubleheader after the break, the Red Sox took care of business 10-0. Then in the night cap, Tampa Bay Rays took an early 2-0 before outfielder Wilyer Abreu decided the next 24 hours were all about him. He hit two home runs on the way to a 5-3 Red Sox win.
The next game was the defining game of the winning streak. The Rays were matching the Sox in scoring all-game before Abreu stepped to the plate down 6-5 in the seventh. Abreu crushed a two-run homer to right field, sending himself and Fenway Park into a frenzy. His fourth home run in 24 hours put Boston up 7-6, a lead they would hold for 12 consecutive wins.
They swept Tampa the next day before taking the first two games of the series versus the Orioles to tie a franchise record 15 straight wins. That first win did not come without drama. A back-and-forth game was knotted up in the eighth when Caleb Durbin smacked a game winning homerun to left field. The “Durbinator” had a rough start to the season but became one of the centerpieces of this win streak.
The streak would end at 15 but just a week later, Boston would rip off another nine straight wins. Durbin hit a walk-off single in an instant classic 12-11 victory against the White Sox. Ceddanne Rafaela became the king of LA for a few days after smacking four home runs in three games against the back-to-back champs.
So here we are, the Red Sox are 84-72 with a firm grip on the second wild card spot in the American League. Now, the New York Yankees stand in their way.
The Yankees beat the Red Sox 2-1 in the three-game wildcard series last year, and Boston is looking for revenge this season.
The pitching will be the key for both teams. Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez will toe the rubber for Boston against the Yankees’ Gerritt Cole, Max Fried and Massachusetts’ own Cam Schlittler in the series.
In his first full season in the MLB, Tolle hit his stride. The southpaw posted a 3.02 ERA and a 10.4 K/9. He is also peaking at the right time, sporting a 0.75 ERA in two starts during September.
In a complete 180 from Tolle, Gray has been dominant in what may be his swan song in the majors. After being acquired via trade in the offseason, Gray has won 17 games, a career high for the veteran. He pitched 7.1 innings of one hit baseball while striking out nine in a June win over the Yankees.
Suarez signed a 5-year $130 million dollar contract with Boston in the offseason and has been solid as a member of the Sox. However, the 2026 all-star struggled in all three of his starts against the Yankees. The Bronx Bombers were 3-0 against Suarez.
Despite great performances by the Yankees, Suarez is a playoff pitcher. He had a 1.48 ERA in 42.2 postseason innings as a member of the Philadelphia Phillies. In Philadelphia’s 2022 run to the World Series, the Phillies won all five games Suarez pitched in. He only allowed two earned runs in 14.2 innings pitched in 2022.
Along with the starters, the back of the bullpen has been nails for Boston. Erik Miller, Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman handled the seventh, eighth and ninth innings for interim manager Chad Tracy and the Red Sox. Miller came over at the trade deadline and did not allow an earned run in his first 10 appearances. Whitlock has been a staple in the Red Sox bullpen since 2021 and is possibly having his best year yet. He has a 1.75 ERA in 53 appearances. Chapman continues to age like fine wine. The 38-year-old was named an all-star for the second straight year and is 34/36 in save situations this year.
The rest of the hitters for the Red Sox will need to do some heavy lifting if they want to compete with the Yankees. Boston acquired Adley Rutschman at the deadline, and the catcher will be required to switch hit and catch in the playoffs. Wilson Contreras and Trevor Story will add postseason experience to the lineup while former top prospect Roman Anthony and local legend Mickey Gasper will look to provide during their first playoff at bats.
If the standings hold, the Red Sox and Yankees will battle in the Bronx on Tuesday for the wildcard series, a statement no Red Sox fan would have believed in June.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Cubs' Alex Bregman pushing for regular-season return after foul ball injury
item.dc:creator: Associated Press
item.description: CHICAGO — Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman could play again in the regular season after he sustained multiple facial fractures when he was struck in the face by a foul ball. Chicago manager Craig Counsell said Bregman did a light workout in the weight room and tracked pitches from a machine in a batting cage. There are no plans to place him on the injured list. "He's still got significant swelling in his face and his eye that needs to improve," Counsell said. "But all things considered, he's in a
item.content:encoded:
CHICAGO — Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman could play again in the regular season after he sustained multiple facial fractures when he was struck in the face by a foul ball.
Chicago manager Craig Counsell said Bregman did a light workout in the weight room and tracked pitches from a machine in a batting cage. There are no plans to place him on the injured list.
"He's still got significant swelling in his face and his eye that needs to improve," Counsell said. "But all things considered, he's in a good place."
Bregman was on deck in the fourth inning of a 9-1 win at Cincinnati when he was hit on the left side of his face on Michael Busch's check-swing foul ball. Bregman immediately jogged toward the Cubs' dugout and covered his face before going back to the clubhouse with an athletic trainer.
"When everything was going down on Sunday afternoon, I think that we all thought the worst case might be a possibility," president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer said. "And all the news since then has been really good. He's had a lot of different doctor's appointments, and they've been positive. And I think we have to take it one step at a time."
Pedro Ramírez started at third in an 8-2 loss to Miami in 12 innings. He went 0 for 5 with two strikeouts. Matt Shaw also could fill in at third while Bregman is out.
Chicago (87-70) can clinch an NL wild card with a win over Miami or a loss by Arizona at Colorado.
The Cubs have five games left in the regular season. But the schedule for their weekend series at Boston is in flux because of heavy rain in the forecast.
"I think Alex is going to be fine. I really do," Counsell said. "The guy is ... he's driving home from Cincinnati and he wants to play. So he's planning on playing. He knew he had to get some good news from the doctors. He got that good news. So he's going to do everything in his power, and as long as I think symptoms don't kind of increase or happen as he increases activity, I think you're going to see him play."
Bregman is batting .262 with 26 homers and 89 RBIs in 153 games during his first season with Chicago. The three-time All-Star signed a five-year, $175 million contract with the Cubs in free agency.
The 32-year-old Bregman got off to a rough start in his new home, hitting just .229 with two homers in his first 20 games. But he has been one of Chicago's most productive players since the All-Star break, batting .305 with 17 homers and 48 RBIs in his last 57 games.
Bregman also has excelled in the postseason in the past. He won two World Series championships with the Houston Astros. He appeared in at least two postseason games in each of the previous nine years.
"To see a friend and a teammate just get hit in the face and bleeding like that is awful," Cubs second baseman Nico Hoerner said. "I think his reactions to everything has been uplifting, just him being relentlessly aggressive and positive and speaking out, all the things that he's excited to do."

item.title: [talksox.com] Chad Tracy Was the Only Man For Red Sox's Manager Job
item.dc:creator: Nick John
item.description: Red Sox Video When the Boston Red Sox relieved Alex Cora of his duties as manager, the team needed someone who could help right the ship and lead a team that was filled with youthful players. The team turned to Chad Tracy, the manager of Triple-A Worcester at the time, giving him the reins to oversee at least the remainder of the season. Now, he’s the official manager of the Boston Red Sox as the team signed him to a contract through the 2029 season with a contract option for 2030. Tracy, a vete
item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Video
When the Boston Red Sox relieved Alex Cora of his duties as manager, the team needed someone who could help right the ship and lead a team that was filled with youthful players. The team turned to Chad Tracy, the manager of Triple-A Worcester at the time, giving him the reins to oversee at least the remainder of the season.
Now, he’s the official manager of the Boston Red Sox as the team signed him to a contract through the 2029 season with a contract option for 2030. Tracy, a veteran manager in the minor leagues where he accumulated 499 wins, oversaw a historic turnaround that saw the team clinch a playoff spot on September 21. Handed a team that had a 10-17 record and that would lose stars Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet shortly after being named interim manager, Tracy's Red Sox dropped all the way to 32-46 on June 24.
Despite that, he never lost faith in his players and appeared to know which buttons to press. With a roster that get huge contributions from Triple-A arrivals, Tracy oversaw a ridiculous 32-5 over their next 37 games to vault them near the top of the American League.
Now, he’ll be around for the foreseeable future.
In all honesty it should have been a no-brainer. Tracy showcased throughout the summer he could handle the pressure of managing in Boston, especially as the team stumbled and faced hardships through most of the season. Despite slip-ups or mistakes made on the field by his players, Tracy was ready to defend them from the media. Never once did he throw a player under the bus or outright say a loss was due to someone’s performance. Even when there were disputes between players that were caught during games or in media sessions, the skipper knew how to keep the heat off his players and kept those issues in-house.
The Red Sox couldn’t have asked for a better manager following Alex Cora's run with the franchise. Both managers have their strengths, but between them, it seems like the current manager is the one best suited to handle a young core.
A young core that he’s already worked with and built relationships with during his time with Worcester, mind you. Of the current active roster, Tracy either managed or oversaw rehab appearances of 16 players (not to mention working with plenty of others in spring training). He’s shown an ability to get the most out of his players and in return the players have given him everything they’re capable of on the field.
For that, Red Sox fans should be happy he’ll be the helmsman of the ship. A guiding hand for the youth on the team while relying on his veterans to support the team in ways only they can.
With playoffs just a week away, it’ll be Tracy's second major test of the season, one that fans may hold as more importance than his ability to turn what once looked like a lost season around. Anyone who’s followed baseball knows that things are different once October rolls around; every decision will be placed under a microscope and sometimes what helped you win in the regular season could make or break championship ambitions.
Heading to New York for a Wild Card series will make things just as rough. Boston lost to the Yankees in three games last season and everyone from the organization to the fan base will be looking for revenge this year. It’ll be Tracy's decisions that could very likely make or break it.
Despite that, fans shouldn’t be too worried about the extension coming without any proven success in the playoffs. After all, previous managers Terry Francona and John Farrell didn’t have success in the playoffs before leading Boston. And Cora’s first managerial experience came in 2018 with the Red Sox, and we all know how that turned out.
Tracy got them here without Roman Anthony or Garrett Crochet for the majority of the season, after all. He’ll face some hardships as manager—every great one does—but he’s shown an ability to remain calm under pressure and push the right buttons to give his team an edge. And for that, Red Sox fans should be excited for the Chad Tracy era to continue.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Red Sox need Ceddanne Rafaela’s return to be immediate solution to slumping offense
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli
item.description: No matter what happens for the rest of the season, the Boston Red Sox are a playoff team — they've popped the bottles and showered in the beer that secures their fate. But Boston's offense hasn't given fans anything to be excited about over the last few games. The Red Sox have lost eight of their last 12 games and three of their last four series, including one to the MLB-worst Los Angeles Angels. Boston has the second-lowest batting average in September (.221) and the sixth-lowest team OPS (.675
item.content:encoded:
No matter what happens for the rest of the season, the Boston Red Sox are a playoff team — they've popped the bottles and showered in the beer that secures their fate. But Boston's offense hasn't given fans anything to be excited about over the last few games.
The Red Sox have lost eight of their last 12 games and three of their last four series, including one to the MLB-worst Los Angeles Angels. Boston has the second-lowest batting average in September (.221) and the sixth-lowest team OPS (.675). It has just a .179 average with runners in scoring position this month. The Red Sox haven't scored more than four runs since their September 12 game against the Kansas City Royals.
Offensive production that minimal won't keep the Sox alive very long in the postseason. Boston will face the New York Yankees in a Wild Card rematch of last season's series, which didn't end well for a highly-injured, slumping team kind of like this year's squad.
Thankfully, offensive reinforcements are coming, starting with Ceddanne Rafaela. The outfielder has been on the 10-day injured list with a strained hamstring since September 3. Red Sox manager Chad Tracy announced following their September 22 loss that Rafaela would be activated the following day.
Red Sox need Ceddanne Rafaela back to help awaken slumping offense
Rafaela has been one of the most important pieces of Boston's offense all year thanks to the best season of his young career. He's slashing .282/.317/.443 with 32 doubles (tied for the 13th-most in MLB), three triples, 16 home runs and 70 RBI over 135 games.
Rafaela isn't the only missing piece of the Sox's offense, as Willson Contreras is also out of commission after taking a pitch to the side of his hand on September 17. Boston's home run leader never went on the IL so he doesn't have to be formally activated to return to action. He's swung a bat and is on the road to recovery, but the Red Sox haven't announced an estimated return date for him.
Rafaela and Contreras being injured can't be an excuse for the Red Sox's offense disappearing with just days to go in the regular season. They could be playing down since the rest of their games don't technically matter, but the sudden decrease in offensive production is concerning nonetheless.
It serves the Red Sox to go into the playoffs confident and with a humming offense. Rafaela's return could help them get there. but the rest of the bats need to step up, as well.

New York has locked up the first wild-card slot, and Boston is closing in on the second. However, the Red Sox are backing into the playoffs. Since the calendar flipped to September, Boston has a 9-10 record after a 3-2 loss to the Cleveland Guardians on Tuesday night at Fenway Park. However, after their torrid July and August, they can afford a bump in the road late in the regular se
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees are on a collision course in next week's American League wild-card round. New York has locked up the first wild-card slot, and Boston is closing in on the second. However, the Red Sox are backing into the playoffs.
Since the calendar flipped to September, Boston has a 9-10 record after a 3-2 loss to the Cleveland Guardians on Tuesday night at Fenway Park. However, after their torrid July and August, they can afford a bump in the road late in the regular season.
Manager Chad Tracy, who had the interim tag removed on Tuesday, had a simple message after a third straight loss, after losing two out of three games over the weekend to the Tampa Bay Rays.
Boston Red Sox Manager Chad Tracy Drops Honest Quote After Loss To Guardians
With not a lot on the line over the final five games for the Red Sox, it's all about gaining momentum heading into the playoffs. Tracy explained his plan for the final five games before they head to the postseason.
"We've still got five games to play, and you (have to) keep guys out there and engaged and ready to roll," Tracy said, per Tim Healey of the Boston Globe. "I told the guys before, we earned the right to be in position to be able to line things up. That being said, we still want to go out and win the games. We had a chance to tonight."
They did have a chance against the Guardians, but they have also earned the right to be in the position they're in. However, what has plagued them in September plagued them on Tuesday night, a struggling offense. They managed to claw back and tie the game at 2-2 in the bottom of the eighth on a Mickey Gaspar solo home run.
Cleveland regained the lead in the top of the ninth inning to secure a huge 3-2 victory. The win kept the Guardians one game ahead of the Chicago White Sox in the race in the American League Central Division. Whoever wins the division likely gets a wild-card round bye, and the loser will visit the American League West Division winner next week for a best-of-three series.
Boston Red Sox Have 5 Games Before the Playoffs Begin
After two more with the Guardians, the Red Sox will then host the Chicago Cubs for three games this weekend. However, just how those games will be played remains to be seen.
There is a nor'easter forecasted to batter the Northeast through the weekend and into next week. Healey reported that MLB was not planning on moving the series out of Boston. There are a couple of avenues they could take, including a potential doubleheader on Friday.
The games have a big meaning for the Cubs. They are in a race with the San Diego Padres and Philadelphia Phillies for home-field advantage in next week's National League wild-card series. MLB needs all three games played one way or another.
Boston wants the games played as well. Gaining some momentum going into the postseason is what Tracy wants. Even if it means moving the schedule around after two more games with the Guardians.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Boston Red Sox Manager Chad Tracy Delivers Honest Quote After Loss To Guardians appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [Away Back Gone] Guardians' late rally poked another hole in Red Sox's suddenly shaky playoff bullpen plan
item.dc:creator: Henry Palattella
item.description: The final week of the MLB season always features plenty of altered and adjusted pitching plans. Normally the one consistent throughout the drumbeat of the 162-game MLB season is a team’s pitching plan; regardless of whether a team has an ace on the mound or is going with pitching madness, the goal is always to get the best position to win while taking it a day at a time. But that's a bit different this week. While some teams are playing out the string and giving their starters one last opportuni
item.content:encoded:
The final week of the MLB season always features plenty of altered and adjusted pitching plans.
Normally the one consistent throughout the drumbeat of the 162-game MLB season is a team’s pitching plan; regardless of whether a team has an ace on the mound or is going with pitching madness, the goal is always to get the best position to win while taking it a day at a time.
But that's a bit different this week.
While some teams are playing out the string and giving their starters one last opportunity to pitch before drifting off into the winter, the teams that have already clinched are stuck in the limbo of trying to cover the now while also preparing for the postseason.
It’s not like football or basketball where you can just throw random backups out there. Every inning needs to be covered, and there’s only so many innings you can give to pitchers who aren’t a part of your postseason plans.
Even if the Guardians won’t be in that position for a couple days (even if they clinch a postseason spot later today the American League Central race still won’t be settled, the Boston Red Sox's already know their postseason fate by virtue of being all but locked into the American League’s No. 5 seed.
We got an early example of how that could change their pitching plans on Monday when manager Andy Tracy pulled budding ace Peyton Tolle after five innings, and we got another example of it later in the game whenTracy went to Erik Miller in the ninth inning of a tied game instead of going to Aroldis Chapman… and Miller gave up the go-ahead run on a Nathaniel Lowe sacrifice fly.
The Red Sox are already playing with their postseason plans in mind, and those plans just got a bit more convoluted thanks to Miller’s rough outing.
The Red sox's bullpen struggles could help the Guardians in their quest to make the postseason
While Miller has largely been excellent since the Red Sox acquired him in August, he’s now allowed a run in three straight appearances and seems to be falling down manager Andy Tracy’s trust tree.
Miller opened his outing by hitting Chase DeLauter on the forearm with a pitch before surrendering a single to Jo Adell that was followed by Lowe’s sacrifice fly.
After the game, Tracy said that Miller was “working through some things,” which was obvious to everyone in the ballpark and watching at home.
Those struggles set up what should be an interesting last two games at Fenway Park. The Sox have two of their best pitchers going in the final two games of the series (Sonny Gray today and Ranger Suarez tomorrow), and it’s hard to believe the Red Sox are going to give them a ton of run in either of their starts.
While the Guardians may not get a chance to benefit from Boston’s relief struggles in the postseason since Boston will likely be locked into the other side of the bracket, they can use it to their benefit over the next 48 hours as they work to nail down a postseason spot.

item.content:encoded:
Curtis Mead Injury: Long shot to play in postseason
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy indicated Tuesday that Mead (wrist) is a long shot to be available for the postseason, Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com reports.
Mead has been sidelined for almost two months with a fractured left wrist that he suffered in his second plate appearance after joining the Red Sox. He began hitting off a tee last week, but his overall progress has been slow and it seems he's likely to run out of time. Mead is under team control through the 2030 campaign.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Announce Ceddanne Rafaela Decision Ahead of MLB Playoffs
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The Boston Red Sox dropped a 3-2 decision to the Guardians on Tuesday night at Fenway Park. The offense managed just two runs on the night and went 0-for-9 with runners in scoring position, continuing a trend that has dogged the lineup for weeks. Boston is 84-73 with five games left in the regular season. The postseason spot is secure. The bats are not where they need to be. The best news of the day had nothing to do with the final score. Tracy Gives Update on Rafaela Red Sox Manager Chad Tracy
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox dropped a 3-2 decision to the Guardians on Tuesday night at Fenway Park. The offense managed just two runs on the night and went 0-for-9 with runners in scoring position, continuing a trend that has dogged the lineup for weeks.
Boston is 84-73 with five games left in the regular season. The postseason spot is secure. The bats are not where they need to be.
The best news of the day had nothing to do with the final score.
Tracy Gives Update on Rafaela
Red Sox Manager Chad Tracy confirmed that Ceddanne Rafaela will be activated from the injured list on Wednesday. The All-Star center fielder has not played since September 2, missing time with a right quadriceps strain.
Rafaela took live at-bats against Garrett Crochet during a bullpen session at Fenway on Tuesday afternoon as a final step before returning. Crochet, working his way back from a left shoulder injury, threw 16 pitches with his fastball sitting in the 94-96 mile-per-hour range.
Rafaela's review of the session was simple.
"Nasty. As always," Rafaela said.
Tracy described Rafaela as "much better" and "getting close" before Tuesday's game. The activation makes it official.
What Rafaela Brings Back
Rafaela has put together the best offensive season of his career. In 135 games before the quad injury, he hit .282 with a .760 OPS, 16 home runs, and 70 RBIs.
The bat matters. So does the glove. Rafaela's range in center field is a genuine difference-maker for a pitching staff that has carried the team down the stretch. His presence in the outfield tightens the Red Sox defense in a way that does not show up in box scores but shows up in results.
The Red Sox have four regular season games remaining after Wednesday before the Wild Card Series begins on September 29. Those reps give Rafaela a chance to shake off the rust and get his timing back before the intensity goes up.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Ceddanne Rafaela is back. The timing is right. The rest of the homestand to get his legs under him, then the postseason.
The Red Sox lineup needs what he provides. Wednesday is the start of getting there.

The post Red Sox Announce Ceddanne Rafaela Decision Ahead of MLB Playoffs appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox SP Payton Tolle Shares Mechanics Concern in Final Regular Season Start

He made his final scheduled start on Tuesday night, throwing 5.2 innings and giving up 2 earned runs in a no decision against the Cleveland Guardians. There was some reason for concern in the start, though. Tolle’s velocity was down. In the first inning, he was hitting around 97 mph on the radar gun. By the second, he was around 94 mph. There were a couple of reasons being suggested, neither of which would be
item.content:encoded:
The regular season has come to an end for Boston Red Sox starting pitcher Payton Tolle. He made his final scheduled start on Tuesday night, throwing 5.2 innings and giving up 2 earned runs in a no decision against the Cleveland Guardians.
There was some reason for concern in the start, though. Tolle’s velocity was down. In the first inning, he was hitting around 97 mph on the radar gun. By the second, he was around 94 mph.
There were a couple of reasons being suggested, neither of which would be good. He could be dealing with the cold, which going into October isn’t what you want to hear. Or, he could have a mechanical issue, which leads to more questions for the young Red Sox pitcher. For his part, Tolle would blame his mechanics.
“I think there was a little bit of just trying to find my legs for a second,” Tolle said. “I think I got very nitpicky. I got trying to be too fine. It’s like, I don’t — you’re going to see the velo dip whenever I’m being too fine. That’s kind of what happened there, especially with those walks. Just trying too hard on some pitches.”
This comes at a time when Red Sox reliever Erik Miller is battling mechanical issues. Those are issues that have led to concerns about what he can be in the postseason. At the very least, Tolle seemed to figure it out midgame.
“So, it is what it is,” Tolle said. “But I think later I got back to just trying to fly through zone and let it be what it be.”
Boston Red Sox Fans Embraced Payton Tolle in 2026
Boston Red Sox fans got their first taste of Payton Tolle in 2025, but he was still a rookie who started 2026 in the minors. It wouldn’t be until injuries hit the rotation that Tolle made it back to the MLB team, which is a tough spot to be in for anyone. Still, he and the fanbase have seemed to embrace each other.
So, it was no surprise that the Fenway Faithful walked him off the mound on Tuesday with a standing ovation. Unless the Red Sox can win a playoff round, that was his final home game of the season.
Tolle wrapped up the regular season with a 3.03 ERA in 26 games and 148.2 innings. He also had a 1.096 WHIP and 10.4 strikeouts per nine. More importantly, he proved he has secondary pitches beyond his fastball, which is still his bread and butter.
Along the way, Red Sox fans embraced Tolle for how he plays the game. He’s both fiery and passionate, but he doesn’t take himself overly seriously. That has seen him hug runners to tag them out, do push-ups after slipping, and smile before throwing an immaculate inning.
The Red Sox Need Tolle for the Postseason
There is no doubt that the Red Sox are going to need Payton Tolle at his best for the postseason. The question is whether or not he’s getting the ball in Game 1. For his part, manager Chad Tracy didn’t want to give anything away just yet.
“TBD,” Tracy said on when Tolle will pitch next. “But good try, though.”
Tolle only got to pitch 0.1 innings last postseason. The Red Sox need more this year from him, and he’s excited for the opportunity.
“I’m excited… I’ll keep going back to how far we’ve come. Go back to June, and what we were thinking sitting in this same room in June. I’m just really proud of this group; this is incredible. I’ve had so much fun— obviously,” Tolle said.

item.title: [Audacy] The story behind Payton Tolle's viral basketball video
item.dc:creator: Rob Bradford
item.description: As if there needs to be more evidence of Payton Tolle's unique likability, along came a reminder from five years ago. That was courtesy of a video showing Tolle as a basketball player from his days at Bethany High in Bethany, Oklahoma. I present to you: The ultimate Payton Tolle highlight video @BBisntBoring pic.twitter.com/qXSZ3rBz5e — Rob Bradford (@bradfo) September 22, 2026 The images came courtesy of a man who witnessed the Tolle Effect first-hand, former Bethany High boys basketball coach
item.content:encoded:
As if there needs to be more evidence of Payton Tolle's unique likability, along came a reminder from five years ago.
That was courtesy of a video showing Tolle as a basketball player from his days at Bethany High in Bethany, Oklahoma.
I present to you: The ultimate Payton Tolle highlight video @BBisntBoring pic.twitter.com/qXSZ3rBz5e
— Rob Bradford (@bradfo) September 22, 2026
The images came courtesy of a man who witnessed the Tolle Effect first-hand, former Bethany High boys basketball coach Quinn Woolridge. Well before the Red Sox were introduced to the personality of the rookie pitcher, Woolridge experienced the unique existence of the former three-sport athlete.
For instance, that hug he gave Seattle's Dominic Canzone three weeks ago was nothing new. Just ask all those basketball coaches who went up against Woolridge and Bethany High went up against and were greeted with Tolle's signature embrace.The kid just had fun doing everything he was doing. Yeah, that was a chance where he could have some fun.
"All the stuff with the highlights that are coming out now, he always been that fun kid," Woolridge told WEEI.com. "I think you guys are probably getting the feel that he is the genuine article. I mean, he's the real deal."
"It's called a highlight reel for a reason," laughed Tolle when talking about the video, that included the lefty nailing three-pointers and throwing down dunks, along with the consistent hugging of opposing coaches. "A little breakway action never hurt anybody. We had a lot of fun."
And as for the coaches' responses to the embraces, "I would say most like it," Tolle explained. "Some f them tried to get away from it, but I was like, 'No, no, come get this. Let the big bird get his paws on here. Word got around. The Oklahoma high school basketball coaches group is small, so they knew."
The influence his basketball years had on Tolle stretched well beyond just those introductory embraces.
Even though baseball was clearly his meal ticket beyond high school, the 6-foot-5 center made a point to put his all into both football and hoop, two sports Woolridge said Tolle could have also had a future in beyond high school.
"Obviously, baseball was his No. 1 sport," the coach said. "I don't think he really even liked football that much, but he was obivously good at it as a tight end and defensive end. And then he literally played basketball like three months out of the year, but he was pretty good. If he wanted to be a basketball player in college, he could have been. If he wanted to be a tight end, he would have been playing on Saturdays (in college) and maybe even Sundays (in the NFL). Being around him, if he wanted to be good at darts, he would have been really good at darts.
"A lot of young basketball guys, they take themselves too serious. They're into a lot of social media stuff and everything. He was a good basketball player, but he didn't take himself too serious and he had a good time with it. He helped everybody else playing that way, too."
While Tolle wasn't Bethany's leading scorer ("They never ran isolations for me," he joked), he was an important part of a very good team. And as much as his presence did for the Bronchos, the reward was just as great for Tolle to get where he finds himself today.
"Every single time a kid or parent comes up to me and says, 'Hey, what advice do you have for my high school?' I tell them to be an athlete because you're going to learn movements and explosiveness. I might not show it out there anymore, but I would say that a lot. Not to too my own horn, but I feel l ike I move fine for a large guy thanks to the base athleticism that was happening in other sports.
"(By playing one sport) you're going to find yourself burned out. You're going to find yourself overusing your muscles over and over again. With basketball, I knew once Christmas and New Year's happened I would go back to throwing after basketball practice, just stacking days. It helped me be an athlete and not get too burnt going to baseball all the time. There's also a lot of mental stuff that goes into, too."
Now, we have the memories, the impact of those days on the basketball court, and a pretty enlightening video montage.
"The biggest thing is he was such a competitor," remembered Woolridge. "He was such a positive influence with all the guys on our team. That was one of my prevailing memories about him.
"You see a lot of guys that have a good PR team that puts good stuff out there about them, and then you meet them in an elevator and they're kind of a turd. What you see with Payton that is out there now is what you get from him every single day, and what he was at Bethany High."

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Is Red Sox pitcher Ranger Suarez postseason ready?
item.dc:creator: Jacob Roy
item.description: If you sign a pitcher to a $130 million contract, you're an MLB decision-maker (Hello! Hire me! I have good ideas and work fairly hard!) If you're not an MLB decision-maker and have the capacity to read my first sentence without taking it literally, you'll want that $130 million pitcher to pitch in big games. item.content:encoded:
If you sign a pitcher to a $130 million contract, you're an MLB decision-maker (Hello! Hire me! I have good ideas and work fairly hard!) If you're not an MLB decision-maker and have the capacity to read my first sentence without taking it literally, you'll want that $130 million pitcher to pitch in big games. The Boston Red Sox signed Ranger Suarez to a 5-year, $130 million contract shortly after losing Alex Bregman to the Chicago Cubs this offseason.
Suarez wasn't making top dollar over the first eight years of his career, but he was pitching in big games. He threw in 11 postseason games for the Philadelphia Phillies, posting a 1.48 ERA on his way to four wins and one save. With one week remaining in the regular season, Suarez is lined up to start game three of the Wild Card series, although Chad Tracy said not to read into that yet. Despite Tracy's guidance, I'm choosing to read into it.
Suarez has been streaky this season. He posted a 2.10 ERA over five starts in June. In August, he registered a 5.70 ERA. If you believe in pitcher streakiness, you'll be pleased to know the lefty has allowed just two earned runs over his last three starts (19.2 innings). Is this the start of a hot streak, or just some fortunate outcomes over a short sample? To quote the owl from the Tootsie Pop commercial, let's find out!
Suarez is typically effective against lefties, although he hit some blips during the middle of the season. He sees mostly right-handed hitters, though the Yankees are likely to keep both Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger in the lineup, as well as potentially Austin Wells and Jazz Chisholm. When Suarez got into trouble against lefties this season, it was primarily by missing the edge of the zone too often, falling behind in counts, and walking hitters. In August, he walked 15% of the lefties he faced. In September, he's only seen 28 lefties, but he's dialed it in.
Suarez has simplified his approach, increasing his sinker and slider usage. He's thrown the sinker on the arm side where it can jam hitters, rather than trying to back door it.
His slider was also located low and on the glove side, which translated to a 50% chase rate. Suarez also increased his first-pitch strike percentage from 55% in August to 68% in September. When Suarez is ahead, hitters are forced to swing at more pitches on the edges, and it translates to easy outs. Bellinger and Rice both hit pitches on the inside part of the plate well. In a few meetings this season, Suarez has opted to pitch primarily away from them. If Suarez does pitch against the Yankees, it will be interesting to see if he tries to jam them or continues to pitch away. Either way, his sinker/slider combination has been very effective over the past few weeks.
Righties are the bigger question for Suarez. Fortunately, the Yankees' right-handed hitters without Aaron Judge in the lineup aren't as daunting. Paul Goldschmidt and Heliot Ramos are the two biggest names, while George Lombard has also hit lefties well in his debut season. Ramos and Lombard each have plenty of strikeouts in their game, as does Jose Caballero. Amed Rosario is also often in the lineup against lefties, but he's posted a wRC+ of just 6 — yes, you read that correctly — 6 against lefties over the past two months.
Back to Suarez. Over his last three starts, he's held righties to a .190 batting average while striking out 24.5% of them. He made some notable changes to his approach as well. He's made changes to both his usage rates and how he's deployed them.
For most of the season, he's led with his cutter against righties. It's been effective, as he's thrown it high and inside where it can jam hitters. In September, he's backed off the usage and thrown it more on the arm side. The strike rate has fallen, but the different approach might be helping his other pitches be more effective.
He's made up for the lower cutter usage by increasing his sinkers to righties. Here's a look at the heat map for most of the season and September.
Early in the season, he almost exclusively kept his sinker away from righties. More recently, he's used the whole plate, throwing it down and away as well as inside. The strike rate is up, while the contact against it is weak. With the cutter more on the arm side, it might be more difficult for hitters to pull the trigger on the sinker, leading to an increase in called strikes.
The other notable change Suarez has made is slashing his changeup usage. For much of his career, his changeup has been his best pitch against righties. The swinging strike rate has been between 15 and 20%, with weak contact against it. This season, the zone rate and chase rate are below his usual marks, leading to a strike rate below 50%. From the beginning of the season through the end of August, the pitch accounted for 17% of his offerings to righties. Over his last three starts, he's used the pitch just 8% of the time. He's thrown it in just four two-strike counts in September, despite it being his second most used pitch against righties for most of the season. While it's a good pitch when it's working, it hasn't been a weapon for most of this season.
Suarez's deep arsenal means it can look very different for him on a given day. After returning from injury in July, he used five pitches over 14% of the time. As the Red Sox inched closer to securing a playoff spot, he cut the changeup and covered that portion of the plate with a sinker. It's an approach that's worked, but could be exposed as hitters are more ready for it. While most of the games this week are largely meaningless, how Suarez approaches righties in his final start of the season is something to watch, and could be a tell for how he performs in the playoffs.

item.title: [nypost.com] Garrett Crochet takes huge step toward Red Sox return ahead of likely Yankees playoff showdown
item.dc:creator: Matt Ehalt
item.description: Garrett Crochet ruined Game 1 for the AL Wild Card series last year for the Yankees. And he could be looking to inflict damage on Boston’s AL East rivals once again. The sidelined lefty ace said he hit 96 mph in a live batting practice session Tuesday and believes he can contribute in the postseason. “The way that … just went, I could go get outs,” Crochet said, according to the Boston Globe. “It depends obviously what role they want me in. item.content:encoded:
Garrett Crochet ruined Game 1 for the AL Wild Card series last year for the Yankees.
And he could be looking to inflict damage on Boston’s AL East rivals once again.
The sidelined lefty ace said he hit 96 mph in a live batting practice session Tuesday and believes he can contribute in the postseason.
“The way that … just went, I could go get outs,” Crochet said, according to the Boston Globe. “It depends obviously what role they want me in. It’s not really for me to say. I know myself and I know my body, and the biggest thing was that I felt good out there. Felt like I was able to ramp up intensity to a place that I haven’t gone yet. Tomorrow is going to be a big deal, seeing how I recover.”
The Yankees and Red Sox are seemingly on a collision course for a second straight Wild Card clash, although Boston has yet to secure the No. 5 seed.
The loser of the AL Central battle between the Guardians and White Sox can still overtake Boston for that date in The Bronx next Tuesday.
Boston entered last postseason with Crochet anchoring its rotation off a season that earned him second place in the AL Cy Young voting but question marks in the rotation after him.
This time around, Boston has established starters but Crochet is the question mark.
Crochet is closing in on five months since he last pitched in an MLB game after landing on the injured list in April with left shoulder inflammation, having last started April 25.
He did not pitch up to his standards in his six outings before being sidelined, posting a 6.30 ERA while allowing 33 hits and five homers in just 30 innings.
It’s uncertain how Boston would use him in the postseason due to the long layoff and the team having quality starters.
Lefties Peyton Tolle, Ranger Suarez and Jake Bennett plus righty Sonny Gray give Boston four capable starters to match up with the Yankees.
Last season, Crochet dominated the Yankees in Game 1, striking out 11 while allowing just one run in 7 2/3 innings in Boston’s 3-1 victory.
Brayan Bello lasted just 2 1/3 innings in a Game 2 loss and rookie Connelly Early logged only 3 2/3 innings in the decisive Game 3 loss.
“He’s definitely making progress,” Boston manager Chad Tracy — fresh off his promotion to full-time skipper — said, per the Boston Globe. “Again, it’s ‘see how he feels tomorrow.’ I know that there’s a lot of conversation around that because we’re only a week away from the postseason now. So determining how does he feel coming out of that [and] what does this weekend look like is going to be the next step.
“What that looks like now, I don’t know. I just know that whatever it is, it’s going to be done with Garrett’s best interest in mind, making sure that we’re doing it right.”
Crochet noted that he would “feel bad” taking someone’s spot on the roster, and said he would accept whatever the front office decides.
With the season ending Sunday, Boston does not have any soft landing spots to allow Crochet to face major-league hitters in a true game environment before the playoffs begin.
Boston ultimately may just have to trust that its star pitcher can return with no hiccups.
“You’re considering all those things,” Tracy said, per the Boston Globe. “We have to consider it and just be very, very mindful of, again, what are we potentially exposing him to and what can he give us really?”

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Red Sox's Ceddanne Rafalea to Return in Significant Development
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: The Boston Red Sox haven't been playing their best overall baseball over the last few weeks in the lead-up to the postseason. Arguably, the biggest reason for this is the fact that they have been navigating a few difficult injuries. For example, center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela hasn't played in a game since Sep. 2 due to a right quadriceps strain. That is expected to change on Wednesday. After the Red Sox's loss against the Cleveland Guardians on Tuesday, Boston manager Chad Tracy shared that Raf
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox haven't been playing their best overall baseball over the last few weeks in the lead-up to the postseason. Arguably, the biggest reason for this is the fact that they have been navigating a few difficult injuries.
For example, center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela hasn't played in a game since Sep. 2 due to a right quadriceps strain. That is expected to change on Wednesday. After the Red Sox's loss against the Cleveland Guardians on Tuesday, Boston manager Chad Tracy shared that Rafaela is expected to be activated off the Injured List on Wednesday and that Willson Contreras has been taking batting practice, as shared on X by The Athletic's Jen McCaffrey.
The Red Sox Are Going To Get A Boost
"Chad Tracy expects Ceddanne Rafaela to be back in the lineup tomorrow. Willson Contreras took BP but still day to day," McCaffrey wrote on X.
Before Rafaela landed on the Injured List, he was smack dab in the middle of the best season of his career to this point. On top of playing Gold Glove Award-level defense in center field, Rafaela was slashing .282/.317/.443 with a .760 OPS, 16 homers, 70 RBIs, 17 stolen bases, 32 doubles and three triples in 135 games played. Rafaela's return shouldn't be understated. This is big news for the Red Sox.
Rafaela has racked up 5.4 wins above replacement this season, which is a new career high. Rafaela has the second-highest total on the Red Sox's roster and is tied for 22nd in baseball in general. If he didn't miss almost a month of action, he'd be much higher as well.
With Rafaela back in the mix, they can slot him in comfortably in center field and near the top of the lineup. With him in center field over guys like Jarren Duran and Nate Eaton. Duran has gotten a chunk of time there since Rafaela got hurt. With center field now full, then it's going to be a question each night whether Boston wants to roll with Duran in left field and Roman Anthony as the DH, or Anthony in left field and then make a decision at DH.
The outfield logjam situation was something that hung over the Red Sox to begin the season. Now, it's a bit different. If the Red Sox were to stick Anthony in left field, there's a good chance that it wouldn't be Duran as the DH. He has shown very solid pop this season, but with five games left, he's batting .204.
Instead, the Red Sox could slide someone, like Mickey Gasper, into the spot. Gasper specifically is batting .259 and bashed his 10th homer of the season on Tuesday. With Rafaela back, Boston's lineup overall can be better. The offense has taken a hit recently, Rafaela is the guy who is going to boost it. Rafaela is going to help himself, and his return could get a struggling bat out of the lineup on a nightly basis. Two positives.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox Pitcher Makes Blunt Admission Amid Recent Struggles
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
