item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ odds of winning the AL East are down to 2.8 percent per FanGraphs after getting walked off by the Diamondbacks last night. I know mathematically that makes sense, but the chances mentally feel even more extreme. I’ve been having “fun” (or whatever) comping the odds to certain pitchers from history getting a hit. We are the dregs. Remember mid-2000s Mets pitcher Aaron Heilman? I personally remember him most for giving up the homer to Yadier Molina late in Game 7 of the 2006 NLCS, just before Adam Wainwright famously caught Carlos Beltrán looking to win the pennant.
Anyway, Heilman was a horrendous hitter. He singled once in his rookie year, and then never got another hit. He ended his career 1-for-47, so an .021 average. So the Yankees just need magic only a little bit more sufficient than that RBI single by Heilman off Sidney Ponson on August 12, 2003! Hell yeah.
It’s not happening, but we press on because it’s good to check up on what everyone else is doing anyway. Here’s what was going on Saturday.
Tampa Bay Rays (94-60) 2, Boston Red Sox (84-71) 1
The Yankees gained a full game on the Rays on Friday for the first time in over a week, as Boston snapped their six-game winning streak. There was no such fortune to be found yesterday though; Tampa Bay made sure of that well before first pitch in Arizona, and it only got worse from there. By the end of the night, the Rays once again had a five-game lead over the Yanks; Tampa Bay’s magic number (combination of Rays wins or Yankees losses) to clinch the AL East is four.
This one was a pitchers’ duel to the bitter end. Brayan Bello had easily his best outing of a turbulent season (and probably the best of his career), firing eight shutout frames at the Trop and fanning 11 Rays, tying a personal best from July 9, 2024. As he only went 5.1 in that one and faced merely the soon-to-depart-Oakland A’s rather than the division-leading Rays.
The only true blemish on Bello’s record came when Jonathan Aranda cracked an opposite-field homer to make it a 1-1 game in the fourth. Tampa Bay had a chance to make it 2-1 against Bello in the seventh when Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson led off with singles. Bello then induced a grounder from Victor Mesa Jr. to move up the runners, and then another off the bat of Richie Palacios to Trevor Story, who nailed pinch-runner Jonny DeLuca at home. Palacios swiped second, but Bello fanned Cedric Mullins to end the inning. The Rays went down in order in the eighth to end Bello’s brilliant night.
Unfortunately for Bello, a win wasn’t in the cards because Boston put up next to nothing against Freddy Peralta and the Rays’ pitching staff. Doubles by Caleb Durbin and Roman Anthony gave the Red Sox their one run in the second, but they were stymied from there. They had chances!
- Second inning after Anthony’s two-out double: Mickey Gasper lineout to center
- Fourth inning with runners on first and second, one out: Story strikeout, Durbin popout
- Fifth inning with runner on second, one out: Anthony groundout, Gasper strikeout
- Sixth inning with runners on first and second, two out: Durbin fly out to left
- Eighth inning after Adley Rutschman’s one-out double: Wilyer Abreu strikeout, Nick Sogard lineout
Even against lockdown Rays closer Bryan Baker, Boston had one last shot to take a late lead. After Story grounded out, Durbin lined a double down the left field line to put himself in scoring position for Jarren Duran. Durbin darted from second, however, and got thrown out stealing third. Duran promptly followed with a triple over DeLuca’s head in center. Isiah Kiner-Falefa bounced one to Junior Caminero at third to end the threat.
Granted a chance to walk it off, Tampa Bay didn’t waste it. Rather than blasting a homer to finish the game as he had twice earlier this homestand, Caminero began the ninth against Garrett Whitlock with a single to left. (A catwalk curtailed Durbin’s effort to catch a popup earlier in the AB.) DeLuca popped up, but Chandler Simpson grounded one through the six-hole for another hit. The runners moved up when catcher Connor Wong let a Whitlock sinker up bounce off his glove for a passed ball. Palacios ended the night with flare to center that fell in, securing the win for Tampa Bay. At least the Wild Card Series is also almost certainly going to be at Yankee Stadium now, I suppose.
AL Rock Fight
Cleveland Guardians (80-75) 12, The Athletics (61-94) 6
Two crooked numbers effectively decided Saturday’s affair with the A’s in a hurry. Tanner Bibee kind of stunk and would allow six runs in a dozen hits while failing to make through five, but it hardly mattered. Cleveland erased a 2-0 deficit in the first on a three-run shot from rookie Chase DeLauter and two-run homer by Angel Martinez. The A’s got one back in the third, only to see another five-spot from the Guardians on poor Jacob Lopez as David Fry, Austin Hedges, and Brayan Rocchio all delivered RBI doubles. Martinez later added a homer and an RBI single in a career-best four-hit day.
Chicago White Sox (79-76) 3, Detroit Tigers (73-82) 1
Cleveland’s win meant that Chicago was stuck at a game back in the AL Central in the best-case, but they did at least help push one of their Wild Card foes out of the picture with a win. Honestly, this was probably kind of a dud of a game for anyone who isn’t a White Sox fan, the lone highlights being Sean Burke’s six scoreless frames and Miguel Vargas’ sixth-inning solo shot to make it 3-1, Chicago (the other runs scored on an RBI single by Munetaka Murakami and a fifth-inning sac fly). Spencer Torkelson had a chance to tie the game with a homer following Hao-Yu Lee’s two-out single in the ninth, but he flew out to center to end it.
Milwaukee Brewers (97-58) 1, Baltimore Orioles (75-80) 0
Yeah, it’s time to stick a fork in the O’s. It was all but certain for awhile now, but Chicago’s win combined with Baltimore’s second-straight loss to Milwaukee means that the Orioles are four back with a week to play, plus multiple teams in front of them. Trevor Rogers was the hard-luck loser here while Baltimore got blanked on four hits and Rece Hinds lost a fly ball from Joey Ortiz in the sun, allowing him to triple and score on Gary Sánchez’s RBI grounder. Woof.
Texas Rangers (78-77) 6, Toronto Blue Jays (76-79) 1
The O’s aren’t the only bird that are all but shot down, either. Trade Deadline acquisition José Soriano coughed up an early homer to Josh Jung, beginning a five-inning, six-run outing that pushed Toronto three games out in the Wild Card and the Rangers into a one-game AL West lead over Houston. The only downside for Texas was that second-half surprise Cal Quantrill—who has a 1.75 ERA since re-entering the rotation in late July—left in the second with lat tightness, so old friend Jordan Montgomery picked up the slack in long relief, retiring 11 of the 12 hitters he faced with no hits allowed.
Atlanta Braves (91-64) 6, Houston Astros (77-78) 3
Houston and Texas have been wrestling all week over the prestigious “Who can win this horri-awful division with a .500-ish record” crown. Sunday it went to Texas with the Astros falling out of their tie for first place (remember that they own the tiebreaker). Isaac Paredes had put Houston ahead with a solo homer and an RBI knock in the third, but the Astros’ bullpen set that lead on fire. The big blow came off the bat of Ronald Acuña Jr., who belted a grand slam off Bryan Abreu in the seventh after AJ Blubaugh made a right mess of things.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] Yankees Birthday of the Day: Tom Tresh
item.dc:creator: Andrew Mearns
item.description: Although a familiar name to scholars of Yankees history (for lack of a better term), Tom Tresh did not have a long big-league career due to injuries and treatment of the time. Nonetheless, he was among the Bombers’ finest players of the 1960s and one of the last gasps of greatness from their vaunted farm system. As the team around him declined, Tresh continued to perform at a high level at multiple positions, making him a fan favorite and a valued final connection to those terrific teams of old.
item.content:encoded:
Although a familiar name to scholars of Yankees history (for lack of a better term), Tom Tresh did not have a long big-league career due to injuries and treatment of the time. Nonetheless, he was among the Bombers’ finest players of the 1960s and one of the last gasps of greatness from their vaunted farm system. As the team around him declined, Tresh continued to perform at a high level at multiple positions, making him a fan favorite and a valued final connection to those terrific teams of old.
Thomas Michael Tresh
Born: September 20, 1938 (Detroit, MI)
Died: October 14, 2008 (Venice, FL)
Yankees Tenure: 1961-69
September 1938 was a big month for the Tresh family, as patriarch Mike made his MLB debut with the Chicago White Sox on September 4th, and son Tom was born on September 20th. Mike Tresh spent 11 years catching for the South Siders, playing in over 1,000 games in the majors until ending his career in 1949 with Cleveland. He was named an All-Star by the Associated Press in 1945, the only year of the 20th century in which the Midsummer Classic wasn’t held (after the creation of the All-Star Game in 1933).
Tom Tresh spent some time living with his parents in an apartment in Chicago, but he went to school in Michigan, as his father’s career was over by then. At Allen Park High School in Detroit, he lettered in baseball, football, and basketball, and he later went to Central Michigan University in Mount Pleasant. His father’s prestigious job allowed him to gain some first-hand perspective on how clubhouses operated and what big-league living was like. He was even allowed to become a bat boy when his father briefly managed at Daytona Beach and Wausau, Wisconsin in 1951 and 1952, respectively.
MLB teams knew just how talented the younger Tresh was, and they kept a close scouting eye on him growing up. Mike and Doris Tresh wanted their son to go to college, but after a year at shortstop in Central Michigan, Tresh felt that he could not turn down a $30,000 offer from the New York Yankees. It was a lot of money for the time, the Yankees were baseball’s marquee team, and like many boys in the ’50s, Mickey Mantle was his idol. He recalled going to Tiger Stadium when the Yankees came to town and watching him intently from the upper deck in center field. Mike had even taught Tom how to switch-hit like Mantle.
Ultimately, Tresh was able to convince his parents to let him sign with the Yankees at age 19, assuring them that he would go back and finish his degree. He was on his way to joining his hero at Yankee Stadium.
Tresh was quick to impress in his first exposure to pro ball in 1958, as he hit .316/.435/.445 for the St. Petersburg Saints in 126 games of Class D ball. His pace slowed down upon a late-season promotion to the Double-A New Orleans Pelicans (no, not them), where the average player was seven years his senior.
It was around this time that Tresh met his idol for the first time, down in spring training. It was recalled in Jane Leavy’s book on Mantle, The Last Boy:
The first time he saw Mantle up close, Tresh was in an elevator during rookie camp in St. Pete--the doors opened and there he was. Though they stood eye to eye, Mantle seemed a thousand steps higher--a feeling Tresh never got over. “I never could see him as just one step higher than I was.”
After batting .246/.363/.415 in 133 games with the Binghamton Triplets in A-ball in 1960, the Yankees tested him at the minors’ highest level. There was no pressure to promote the young prospect, as the big-league club was in the midst of one of their greatest seasons in history, a 109-win romp to the World Series powered by Mantle and Roger Maris. Tresh had a superb year in his own right, hitting .315/.380/.428 in 141 games at shortstop with Richmond and taking home International League MVP honors.
As a reward of sorts, Tresh was tabbed for his MLB debut as a September call-up in ‘61. With another Rookie of the Year-turned-regular in Tony Kubek at shortstop ahead of him, it was hard to find time. Tresh did make it into nine games though, debuting on September 3rd as a pinch-runner and taking his first at-bat on September 16th in his hometown at Tiger Stadium. Tresh notched his first big-league hit in the first game of a doubleheader on September 26th against the Orioles. The huge story that day was Maris tying Babe Ruth with his 60th homer of the season, but Tresh played his part as well, singling to right field off Jack Fisher in the middle of a rally that put the Yankees in front.
Tresh was only technically part of a championship team in ‘61, but the next year, he truly earned his ring. An opportunity arose, as Kubek was recalled to the U.S. Army Reserve. Manager Ralph Houk entrusted the starting role at shortstop to Tresh over fellow infielder Phil Linz. It was the right call, as Tresh went on to an All-Star rookie campaign. He capably fielded the position in Kubek’s absence while hitting well from both sides of the plate. Tresh racked up 20 homers and a .286/.359/.441 triple slash, good for a 119 wRC+, Rookie of the Year honors, and even a 12th-place finish for MVP.
There was the potential for an awkward situation to arise when Kubek returned from the service in August, and Houk tasked Tresh with playing alongside Mantle in left field. In 573 minor-league games, Tresh had never manned the outfield, but he handled it with aplomb. Having previously made that same transition, Mantle even gave Tresh his glove, choosing to befriend and praise his potential future replacement rather than ignoring him, as Joe DiMaggio did to Mantle. Tresh knew Mantle had his flaws, but he loved him anyway and eventually nicknamed his son “Mickey” for him in 1964. (“What the fuck did you do that for?” Mantle later asked. He knew he was no idol.)
The Yankees won the pennant and played the San Francisco Giants in the World Series. Tresh had only just turned 24 and yet he didn’t appear to be fazed at all. He hit .321/.345/.464 in the seven-game series, leading the Yankees in hits and average. It wasn’t garbage time participation either, as his three-run homer in the eighth off Jack Sanford gave the Yankees a Game 5 victory,
Mike Tresh was in the stands at Yankee Stadium when Tresh hit that homer to win Game 5, crying tears of joy. His son had definitely made it.
A terrific one-handed catch by Tresh on a seventh-inning Willie Mays drive in Game 7 likely saved a run with the red-hot Willie McCovey on deck. The Yankees edged the Giants 1-0 to bring home their 20th championship.
Rather than suffering a sophomore slump in ‘63, Tresh had an outstanding year. He was on fire, hitting .269/.371/.487 with 25 dingers and a career-best 141 wRC+. Tresh was an All-Star for the second year in a row and again earned down-ballot MVP votes as the Yankees ran away with the AL pennant thanks to 104 victories. Tresh spent the year in the outfield and even manned center while Mantle missed a few months due to injury. Unfortunately, they had no answer for the overwhelming Los Angeles Dodgers pitching staff in the World Series. Tresh managed to take the seemingly untouchable Sandy Koufax deep late in Game 1, but like most of his team, he was otherwise quiet. They swept the Yankees away.
Houk moved up to the front office in 1964 and the popular Yogi Berra took over in the dugout. The Yankees won their fifth straight pennant, but it was as tough a climb to the top as the team of that era ever endured. They battled injuries and ineffectiveness from several positions, including Kubek at shortstop. Tresh remained a solid player, though he also saw his numbers slip. The Yankees faced a tough competitor in the Cardinals, and it was a tight seven-game series. Tresh slugged .636 and homered twice, including a game-tying blast off World Series MVP Bob Gibson in the ninth inning of Game 5.
It wasn’t enough, as the Cardinals prevailed and Berra was stunningly fired.
The Yankees pulled off a classic “if you can’t beat him, sign him” move for ‘65 by hiring Johnny Keane, who just beat them in the World Series. Kubek played poorly at shortstop and missed a lot of time, but Keane kept Tresh in the outfield, alternating him between relieving Mantle in center and playing left (there was even some right mixed in). To some extent, it paid off, as Tresh finished in the top 10 for AL MVP, won a Gold Glove, and showed no sign of ill-effect at the plate with a 136 wRC+. To another extent, it didn’t, as the team around him was not good; the Yankees fell below .500 for the first time in 40 years.
Despite the increasing effects of a pitching-heavy era, Tresh pulled off a career-high in home runs in ‘66, smacking 27 dingers in 151 games. That was one of the few highlights for the Yankees though, who were abysmal and dropped all the way to last place. Keane was fired and replaced by Houk in May, who moved Tresh to third base since he wanted to give a young Roy White time in the outfield. Tresh ended up splitting time between left and the hot corner. The Yankees appreciated his athleticism and Zobristian ability to handle basically any position, but it still mystified Tresh to a certain degree:
“I win Rookie of the Year as a shortstop and they move me to the outfield. Then I win a Gold Glove Award there in 1965 and they move me to third. I couldn’t figure out what position I was supposed to prove I could play.“
Although Tresh was only 28 entering the 1967 campaign, the second game of spring training was the beginning of the end. He popped his right knee while firing a throw across his body from left field to the cutoff man. Tresh was in serious pain and could barely walk; it was later revealed to be torn cartilage. Inexplicably, the Yankees told him that he should try to play on it rather than undergo surgery.
It was a disaster. Through some miracle, Tresh kept his numbers above league-average with a 106 wRC+, but his OPS dipped below .700 and he was a shadow of the defender he once was in left field. Tresh later recalled that his knee “gave out five more times” that year, undoubtedly affecting his future. He had surgery to repair the damage in the offseason (why he wasn’t simply shut down on a 90-loss team is a mystery), but the damage was done. Tresh was mostly a hobbling shortstop in ‘68 and his play only worsened in ‘69.
By then, the only other position players aside from Tresh remaining from the Yankees’ early ’60s glory were Joe Pepitone and catcher Jake Gibbs. Mantle, Maris, Berra, Kubek, Elston Howard, and Bobby Richardson were all gone. Tresh was miserable. The team was middling at best, and he could barely hit, let alone play shortstop. So he asked if the Yankees would trade him to the Tigers, where he could at least be close to home, not to mention play for the defending World Series champions. The Yankees acquiesced, and Tresh was dealt to Detroit on June 14th. The very next person to wear number 15 for the Yankees was a worthy heir: Thurman Munson.
Tresh remained primarily a shortstop and appeared in 94 games for the Tigers, batting .224/.305/.387 with 13 homers, a .692 OPS that was amusingly still good for a 92 wRC+ in the league-wide offensive malaise. While Detroit was a better team, there was still no competing with the 109-win juggernaut Orioles, who ran away with the AL East in the first year of divisional play.
Tresh had gone through another surgery on his knee in hopes of playing again in 1970. However, the Tigers told him that he would need to rehab in the minors, and Tresh had no intention of living that kind of life again, particularly with a wife and four kids at home. So Tom Tresh retired having played just eight games after his 31st birthday. His story was a warning sign about the dangers of dismissing injuries, but he had no regrets.
Even though Tresh was so talented before his injury that the Red Sox briefly considered a swap of him for Carl Yastrzemski, one can’t blame Tresh for his overall happiness about his career. He was a beloved teammate, a World Series champion, an All-Star, and an MVP candidate for baseball’s greatest franchise. At the time of his retirement, he was even in the Yankees’ all-time top 20 in homers at 140 (the recent offensive spike pushed him back to a tie for 34th as of 2026). Tresh had a fine life post-retirement too, as he did fulfill that college promise to his parents, even after his father’s passing in 1966.
Tresh earned his degree in physical education from Central Michigan in 1969, where he later served as an assistant baseball coach for 15 years and helped innovate a training tool for sliding and diving called the Slide-Rite. His son Mickey inherited the baseball gene, playing at Miami University of Ohio before going through four years in the minors as well with New York and Detroit. The younger Tresh even got a glimpse of the ascendance of one of the great successors to Tresh and Mantle in center: his 1988 Prince William Yankees teammate, 19-year-old Bernie Williams.
The bond between the Mantles and Treshes remained strong—the two Yankees were at a card show in Nashville when Mickey Tresh called to inform his father that he just had a boy of his own, who he named Tommy. Mantle celebrated with Tresh by ordering a $150 bottle of Dom Perignon, raising a toast to the lad, and later writing “Happy birthday Tommy, we had one for you. Mickey Mantle.” on the bottle.
That bottle could have sold for something valuable, as the glove Mantle gave to Tresh in 1962 was enough by itself to put a down payment on a cottage. Tom Tresh never sold it though; it meant too much to him, and he grieved as much as any of his teammates on the day Mantle passed away from liver cancer in 1995. Thirteen years later, Tresh suddenly left the world as well, as he died of a heart attack on October 14, 2008, not even a month after turning 70.
At least Tresh got to see the old Yankee Stadium one last time before it closed for good, as he was in attendance at the final Old-Timers’ Day. As always, the crowd gave him an ovation before he stepped to foul line one last time. Number 15 will always mean Thurman Munson, but it will also always be connected to Tommy Tresh, another fantastic Yankee.

item.content:encoded:
There just haven’t been enough games like Saturday’s for the Cubs this year. It wasn’t easy. It never is with this team if they aren’t scoring 10 plus runs. But the pitching was really good save for one rough inning in the fifth that probably wasn’t as bad as it looked, aided by a weird, bad throw from Dansby Swanson on a relay play. That led to one of the two runs that the Cubs did allow in this one to being unearned. Daniel Palencia followed and was terrific. Aaron Civale was a little shaky. Ryan Zeferjahn is really tough to watch despite clearly immense talent. I’ve not followed his career and haven’t dug into it, but without doing so, I can confidently say that every coach he’s ever has dreamed of a fully unlocked Zeferjahn who might be a truly elite pitcher. Ryan Rolison faced one batter, doing his job and recording a save.
Fun fact, this team has allowed exactly two runs 34 times this year. They are 26-8 (.765) when they do so. I was surprised it was so many games, given the struggles of this pitching staff. They’ve allowed two or fewer 50 times. They have a record of 42-8 in those games. If you mentally shed a tear for this team not having a healthy dose of 2024 Justin Steele, 2025 Cade Horton or 2026 Ben Brown, this is why. I heard it said on the Marquee pregame Saturday that this position player group should have led to a 100-plus win team. It felt so bold. But it’s totally true. With reasonable pitching, this is a 100-plus win team. And that’s why the postseason is not completely hopeless. If they get some pitching, they can win.
On the other side of the ball, the Cubs turned eight hits and three walks and a hit batter into five runs. So slightly less traffic than the night before, but one more run. Two homers and not one. A double to go with it. But more than anything, it was just clustering things together a little better. For the second straight night, the Cubs got largely nothing out of the duo of Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman, who have led the way for this team, particularly in the second half. The rest of the lineup was pretty balanced and the offense was a team effort.
It’s been a week now since the last double-digit offensive game. It’s probably not worth a lot of mention, but it seems like the Cubs get one of those every week or 10 days. So that’s probably coming somewhere in the near term. It would be nice to get one of those easier ones and not to have to sweat every inning as this team closes in on clinching a playoff spot and tries to secure the top Wild Card. Regardless, the Cubs will have a chance to win a third straight series on Sunday afternoon and that’s what you want to see. It’s been a welcome bounceback after the nightmare in Milwaukee. As I said following that last game there, this team is very professional. They’ll bounce back and this won’t linger. It was a really good time to be right.
With any luck, this team will just keep on winning series as the season winds down. Win Sunday afternoon, get home and take a series from a Marlins team that is fighting down to the wire despite being eliminated. The Marlins are in San Diego and we’ll catch them coming back east after playing there and in Arizona. That’s a tough trip. Especially when the clock strikes midnight on your season mid trip. Nine-game trips are always hard. But three good teams, a couple of different time zones (that are both different from their home time zone), different styles of play. It’s a lot. Then the Cubs get a Red Sox team that is pretty squarely locked into the second Wild Card spot. They’ll want to be lining up pitching for their Wild Card series which very likely will be against the Yankees. Of course, the Cubs will be getting theirs set too. But the gap between one and six for Cub starters just isn’t massive (which is damning with faint praise).
Anyway, it was a good night in Cincinnati. Seiya Suzuki seems to be coming out of a slump a little bit. Three singles in the last two games. Only one really hit hard, but using the field and having some success. Michael Busch hit a monster homer. Dansby Swanson had his rehab washed out, but save for the weird throw, he looked like he’s ready to contribute. He had a single and a homer of his own. Good to get Dansby back. It’s his defense that provides most of his value. But, Dansby has the mind and approach of a superstar. He doesn’t shy from the biggest moments. That’s not a bad bat to have down at eight or nine in your lineup. This team is better with Dansby on the field. Just as it usually is with Ian Happ on the field. A player need not be a Superstar to produce consistent positive value for a team.
Three Positives:
- Daniel Palencia faced six batters in the sixth and seventh inning. That sixth inning was huge with just a one-run lead and the 2-3-4 hitters due up for the Reds. He was fairly efficient and got a second inning of work. He’s looked better the last couple of times and is maybe re-finding himself just in time.
- Dansby Swanson had a single and a homer, scored twice.
- Michael Busch had a single, a homer and was hit by a pitch. He scored once. He had a really nice homestand before this trip (.316/.417/.526). He hasn’t really hit a groove all year long. Maybe he too is hitting his peak at just the right time?
Game 155, September 19: Cubs 5, Reds 2 (86-69)
Reminder: Heroes and Goats are determined by WPA scores and are in no way subjective.
THREE HEROES:
- Superhero: Michael Busch (.208). 2-3, HR, HBP, RBI, R
- Hero: Daniel Palencia (.197). 2 IP, 6 BF, 3K
- Sidekick: Seiya Suzuki (.128). 2-3, BB, RBI
THREE GOATS:
- Billy Goat: Tyrone Taylor (-.125). 0-3
- Goat: Carson Kelly (-.094). 0-4
- Kid: Pete Crow-Armstrong (-.082). 0-5
WPA Play of the Game: Michael Busch hit a solo homer with one out in the sixth to give the Cubs a one run lead. (.167)
Reds Play of the Game: JJ Bleday singled with a runner on first and one outs, the Reds down two in the fifth. This is the play where Dansby Swanson threw it past Alex Bregman at third, allowing a run to score. (.149)
Cubs Player of the Game:
Game 154 Winner: Carson Kelly received just 17 of 43 votes, but with very divided voting, that was enough to win.
Rizzo Award Standings: (Top 5/Bottom 5)
The award is named for Anthony Rizzo, who finished first in this category three of the first four years it was in existence and four times overall. He also recorded the highest season total ever at +65.5. The point scale is three points for a Superhero down to negative three points for a Billy Goat.
- Alex Bregman +25
- Pete Crow-Armstrong +22.5
- Carson Kelly +17.5
- Shōta Imanaga +15
- Ben Brown +13.5
- Jameson Taillon -13
- Nico Hoerner -16
- Dansby Swanson -17
- Seiya Suzuki -17
- Caleb Thielbar -17.5
Scoreboard Watching: The Phillies lost for the second straight night. They fall one game behind the Cubs, while the Padres won and are tied with the Cubs. The Cubs hold tiebreakers over both teams. The Diamondbacks won a game started by Cam Schlittler, finding some offense against him and then walking it off to win. The Arizona win delays the eventual Cub playoff clinch. That’s two this week as they try to keep their very narrow playoff hopes alive. Even with the win, they remain four games behind the Phillies for the last playoff spot.
Up Next: The Cubs finish the series with the Reds. David Peterson (8-8, 5.11) starts for the Cubs. David is 2-1 with a 4.31 over his last seven, including a win last time against the Braves, allowing a run on three hits and three walks over six innings. The general trend for Peterson is about four good starts to every bad one and they are very stratified. So once he gets it going, he usually delivers. Look to see if he can get locked in early in Cincy. Certainly a guy who likes to keep the ball down is a welcome choice in that park. He held the Reds to two runs over five at Wrigley at the end of August. But they also saw him twice as a Met and did quite well against him (nine runs in eight innings of work).
24-year-old Rhett Lowder (6-11, 5.79) has had a rough first full year as a starter (27 appearances, 24 starts). The strain of a long season may be weighing him down as the year draws towards a close. He’s 2-4 with a 7.13 over his last seven games. He’s allowed 45 hits and 12 walks in just 35.1 innings over those seven starts. The Cubs have seen him twice as a starter and once as a reliever. As a starter, he’s allowed six runs in just eight innings of work. The two relief innings were scoreless, though he issued two walks. He and Peterson faced each other in that game in August. Lowder won, despite allowing three runs over five innings. He did a good job that night staying in the strike zone, not walking anyone (the only time he’s done so since July). He hasn’t won since that start at the end of August, losing all three starts (Brewers, Dodgers, Dodgers, ouch).
Get the offense going early and see if you can post some crooked numbers and ride that to a win. Don’t let Lowder settle in and find some of what made him a 7th overall pick in 2023. He’ll probably eventually be a good starter. But how about not now?

item.content:encoded:
Happy Sunday, folks. Given the results around the league last night, it appears that the Red Sox's magic number to clinch the postseason is down to one. The Rangers can get to 85 wins, while the Astros can get to 84. If the Rangers were to get to 85 wins, they'd clinch the American League West. If they sit at 84, the Red Sox own that tiebreaker. The Astros hold the tiebreaker over the Red Sox, so if Boston were to lose its final seven and Houston were to win its final 7, the Red Sox would trail them in the standings. That's not accounting for the third and final spot, but I won't try to litigate that.
Long story short, win one game, and you've got yourself a Wild Card spot. It's that simple. Except it's not, because Patrick Sandoval is scheduled to pitch today, and he's not very good. The Rays are throwing Griffin Jax, who has a 3.40 ERA since moving to the rotation, but has struggled against the Red Sox in two starts this season. Most recently, he allowed 7 earned runs in five innings.
With the Patriots on today and a questionable pitching matchup, I'm not expecting a lot of eyes on the Red Sox this afternoon. Winning your way into the postseason is always fun, however, so let's hope we can get that celebration in Tampa tonight. If not, the Red Sox will return home to Fenway for their final homestand of the regular season on Tuesday.
First pitch at 1:40 pm on NESN and WEEI.

item.title: [Just Baseball] Payton Tolle’s Case To Be the Red Sox's Game 1 Starter | Just Baseball
item.dc:creator: Jordan Leandre
item.description: They haven’t clinched a postseason berth yet, but it looks more likely by the day that the Boston Red Sox have a date with the New York Yankees in the Wild Card round again. This will be the third matchup between these two arch rivals in the Wild Card round since 2021, with each organization winning once. item.content:encoded:
They haven’t clinched a postseason berth yet, but it looks more likely by the day that the Boston Red Sox have a date with the New York Yankees in the Wild Card round again.
This will be the third matchup between these two arch rivals in the Wild Card round since 2021, with each organization winning once. The Red Sox got the best of Gerrit Cole in 2021 at Fenway Park, while the Yankees won two straight elimination games to knock off Boston in the Bronx last year.
This series promises to be low-scoring. These two teams are top three in baseball in staff earned run average. The Yankees have nearly three-quarters of a run lead on the Red Sox among starters, while the two bullpens are separated by 0.01 earned runs per nine.
A lot will be made of how these two staffs line up in a couple of weeks. The first two games for the Yankees, as deep as their pitching staff is, seem destined to be Cam Schlittler in Game 1 and Max Fried in Game 2. However, the Red Sox have serious questions to answer about how they want to line up.
Preparing for this series to go the distance is difficult. If you sweep, you line yourselves up well for Game 1 of the American League Division Series. However, if you get swept, one of your best pitchers may never see the hill.
The conundrum is as follows: Sonny Gray has been their best arm wire-to-wire. Payton Tolle is by far their hottest arm, seeming to get stronger as the season wears on. Ranger Suárez is riding two great starts in a row and is their high-priced free agent with elite postseason pedigree.
But of the three, there’s no question who should pitch opposite Schlittler in Game 1: Tolle.
Stats updated prior to games on September 19.
Game 1 Is a Tone-Setter
The dialogue surrounding Game 1 is that it’s almost a “scheduled loss.” To be frank, it’s hard to argue against the logic. In four starts against Boston this year, Schlittler has a 0.74 ERA, a .174 batting average against, and a 27.3% strikeout rate across 24.1 innings.
Let us not forget the sheer domination he exhibited in Game 3 against the Red Sox last year, either. Across eight innings, he allowed five hits, no runs, and struck out 12.
But the mindset for Boston can’t be that it has no chance of winning. Sure, they’ve been one of the league’s best road teams this year, but the Yankees have the best pitching staff in baseball this year for a reason. By comparison, sure, it’s easier to win against someone not in the Cy Young race. But Max Fried habitually finds himself in the discussion for a reason.
The Red Sox’s mindset should be that runs will be at a premium, so matching the Yankees ace zero-for-zero is paramount. Of the three options, Tolle presents the best opportunity to do so. While Gray has Tolle beat overall in ERA, the Red Sox rookie southpaw is, by far, the hottest arm on the staff.
Since the All-Star break, Tolle has a 2.90 ERA with a 28.2% strikeout-to-walk rate. That ERA drops to 2.53 over his last nine starts. That 2.90 ERA, however, is nearly a third of a run better than Gray’s, and over half a run better than Suárez’s.
Sheer run prevention is the name of the game in this series. Tolle is their best option.
Tolle’s Attitude Is Perfect for the Moment
Every time Tolle speaks, he endears himself to the baseball world even more. But as goofy as he can be in media sessions, he’s all business on the field. Furthermore, he can appreciate the moment he’s in at any given time.
Look no further than his recent start against the Kansas City Royals. Eight pitches, eight strikes, six whiffs, all fastballs. He had the wherewithal to glance at pitching coach Andrew Bailey, grin, lock back in and pick up the final strike of an immaculate inning.
Sure, it’s one pitch in the first inning against a team out of postseason contention, but talk to anybody who’s played, and they’ll tell you how aware they are of when they’re on the brink of something cool. Tolle said as much after the game.
But that moment should tell the world he’s unafraid of going into the Bronx, facing off against Schlittler, and going band-for-band with the likely AL Cy Young.
Tolle clearly cares about what he does, but it’s that somewhat unserious attitude that makes him perfect for the high stakes of setting the tone in a postseason series.
This moment, honestly, seemed set in stone the moment he made his MLB debut last season against Paul Skenes. While any postseason start is high leverage, he’s always finding himself making big starts against the game’s best. He’s always met the moment, and the Red Sox should let him continue that trend this postseason.
The Yankees Struggle Against Hard Fastballs
The Yankees are a deep, talented team even if not all players are at full strength or potential going into October. One area where they struggle, however, is against hard fastballs.
This season, the Yankees have the highest strikeout rate on fastballs 95 mph or harder, to go with the second-worst expected batting average. Only the Chicago White Sox are worse against such fastballs.
They’re even worse this season on hard fastballs thrown by left-handers. Their 33% strikeout rate is the second-highest behind the 61-93 Athletics, while their .191 expected batting average ranks only higher than the Cleveland Guardians.
Tolle isn’t positioned with an elite-level fastball from a velocity standpoint, but it’s comfortably above average. This season, he’s in the 71st percentile with an average fastball of 95.7 mph. Opponents struggle mightily against it as well, hitting just .190 with a .248 expected wOBA and a 30.4% whiff rate.
Tolle throws his four-seam and sinker a combined 68.4% of the time. While that leaves him susceptible to predictability, he varies that look with a cutter that comes in at 88.6 mph on average. He throws that offering at a 19.4% clip.
His strength is his fastball, along with 98th percentile extension. That plays directly into the weaknesses of the Yankees lineup. With Game 1 very much being a tone-setter, there’s no question who the Red Sox should send out there.
Lining It Up After Tolle
Following Tolle, the Red Sox have their two veterans waiting in the wings. Win Game 1, you’ve got two proven performers to help you win one more game to advance. Lose Game 1, you’ve got two experienced professionals tasked with staving off elimination.
The order after Tolle almost doesn’t matter. Could they vary looks and go to Gray to keep the Yankees off the lefty scent? Maybe, but then you potentially run into the same problem of playing with your food. That said, Suárez is much craftier than Tolle, and prone to the hanging breaking ball.
The Yankees have a 99 wRC+ as a team against right-handed pitching, and a 107 against lefties. Gray also took a no-hitter into the eighth inning against the Yankees back in late June, while Suárez was touched up in his last start against them.
What can be said either way is that having two accomplished veterans to follow the rookie gunslinger is a good position for the Red Sox to be in.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

20 Sep 2026, 20:35 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Kim Klement Neitzel)
Jahmai Jones said he feels the Boston Red Sox have grown this week, and perhaps he has a point.
After Trevor Story's late homer led Boston to a win in the finale of its previous series, the Red Sox will look to capture the decisive contest of their current set on Sunday against the Tampa Bay Rays in St. Petersburg, Fla.
Jones homered from the designated hitter position in Friday's 4-2 victory over the Rays. He said the two games more resembled the way Boston has played during the second half of 2026.
'We've had some big performances. I feel like it's a different guy every night,' said Jones, who notched his sixth homer of the season in a night in which Roman Anthony went deep and had three RBIs.
'Everybody in here knows what we're playing for. I feel we've had a lot of tight ball games. That last one in Texas (on Thursday) and then (Friday showed) who we are and what our baseball is.'
The Red Sox (84-71) saw their momentum slowed on Saturday, however, with a 2-1 setback to the Rays (94-60). They enter the game comfortably in line for the second wild card in the American League.
Richie Palacios had an RBI single in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero with the winning run. It marked the third walk-off win of the season-ending homestand for Tampa Bay.
'We're just relentless. No matter what's going on in the game, we always feel like we have a chance to win,' Palacios said. 'Three walk-offs is amazing, and we're just going to continue to do what we do.'
Tampa Bay has won seven of its past eight games overall to move five games ahead of the second-place New York Yankees in the American League East. The teams each have eight games remaining on their schedule -- four of them against each other. The teams open their series Tuesday in New York with a doubleheader.
'It's very encouraging. It's a good feeling,' Rays manager Kevin Cash said following Saturday's game. 'You want to get as many reps at that as possible, because we know the games that we're going to continue playing this year are going to be against good teams and in tight ballgames.'
Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA) is scheduled to start on Sunday.
Jax scattered two hits over five scoreless innings and struck out seven in five innings of a no-decision against the Athletics last Tuesday. The Rays won 2-1.
He is 0-1 with a 9.00 ERA in two starts against Boston this season. He is 0-2 with a 7.86 ERA in 16 career appearances (three starts) against the Red Sox.
Boston left-hander Patrick Sandoval (1-6, 4.99) is the scheduled starter on Sunday. He has lost his past six decisions heading into Sunday's game, most recently a 4-2 setback to the Texas Rangers on Tuesday. He yielded four runs on four hits in 2 2/3 innings and threw 68 pitches.
Sandoval is 0-3 with a 3.67 ERA in nine games (eight starts) against the Rays.
The Red Sox would love to welcome back Ceddanne Rafaela, who suffered a right quadriceps strain on Sept. 2 in a game against the Seattle Mariners and was placed on the 10-day injured list. He was hitting .282 with 16 home runs, 32 doubles and 70 RBIs to go along with 17 stolen bases.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox will face off against the Tampa Bay Rays on Sunday in a rubber match on the road and the Red Sox got a reinforcement back just in time for the series finale.
Boston has been missing 2026 breakout flamethrower Tyron Guerrero since Aug. 31. That will change on Sunday afternoon. The Red Sox announced that Guerrero is back and righty Wyatt Olds has been sent down to Triple-A in response.
"The Red Sox today reinstated RHP Tyron Guerrero from the 15-Day Injured List. To make room, Boston optioned RHP Wyatt Olds to Triple-A Worcester," the Red Sox announced.
The Red Sox Got A Key Back
Over the last few weeks, much has been said about the reinforcements coming. Guerrero's return is the first example of this. The 6'8'' righty has a 3.26 ERA and a 36-to-7 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 38 2/3 innings pitched. It had been seven years since Guerrero had pitched in a big league game before the 2026 season. He last pitched in the majors back in 2019 with the Miami Marlins. He's been a breakout story for the Red Sox and now he's back.
Olds has been very good when he has been active on the big league roster this season. He has a 1.20 ERA in 13 appearances this season as a rookie, to go along with a 20-to-7 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 15 innings pitched.
Guerrero is the first reinforcement back for the bullpen, but he isn't likely to be the last. Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck are two other guys who could be back in the not-so-distant future. Houck is closer than Crochet is. Houck has been on a minor league rehab assignment. Crochet has been tossing bullpens, but hasn't advanced to facing live hitters just yet.
Olds has been good, but it was known that difficult bullpen decisions would be coming. This is the first and we should see more in the coming days.
Guerrero went from unknown among the Red Sox's fanbase, to a high-leverage guy for Boston fairly quickly. Now, he's back as Boston has a chance to clinch a spot in the postseason on Sunday afternoon against the Rays. If the Red Sox take down Tampa Bay, they will officially punch their ticket. Boston's magic number is down to one. A win will get them into the playoffs. Even if they lose, they can make it in on Sunday with losses by other clubs fighting for the Wild Card spots. It could be a big day for Boston and Guerrero's back.

item.description: Curtis Mead has arguably been the most frustrating non-factor for the Boston Red Sox this season, because he never got his chance to make an impact. In his very first game after being acquired in a trade with the Washington Nationals, Mead fractured his left wrist on a high-and-tight fastball against the Athletics. item.content:encoded:
Curtis Mead has arguably been the most frustrating non-factor for the Boston Red Sox this season, because he never got his chance to make an impact.
In his very first game after being acquired in a trade with the Washington Nationals, Mead fractured his left wrist on a high-and-tight fastball against the Athletics. He quickly found himself in an uphill battle to return to action before the Red Sox's season ended at some point in the playoffs, but he's started making some progress.
According to a Saturday MLB.com injury update, Mead has begun hitting off a tee, which slipped under the radar amid a slough of injury news about Willson Contreras, Garrett Crochet, and others. Good news, to be sure, but far from a guarantee he makes it back for a game this year.
Mead's return not imminent, but progress made
Interim manager Chad Tracy said earlier this week that the tee work was beginning on Wednesday, per Boston Sports Gordo on X. That means we're a few days late to this particular story, so apologies to our readers — but not much slips by us, so it was a particularly quiet announcement.
Mead's breakout season (.851 OPS, 17 home runs in 88 games) was halted at the worst possible time. The Red Sox were looking to add an impact bat at the trade deadline, and Mead's absence has been nearly as awkward as Adley Rutschman's struggles.
Would Mead be the slam-dunk starter at second base even if he came back fully healthy this week? That's another real issue to consider, since Nick Sogard has done a nice job over the last month-plus. Perhaps Mead would at least be in the lineup against left-handed pitchers over the struggling Andruw Monasterio and/or Isiah Kiner-Falefa.
The Red Sox will have interesting decisions to make at the fringes of the roster for the first couple of rounds of the playoffs, no matter what. If Mead re-enters the picture, we could see someone who feels like they earned their spot get the axe, but that's the cost of doing business in a year when the American League could be up for grabs.
Jackson Roberts is a former Division III All-Region DH who now writes and talks about sports for a living. A Bay Area native and a graduate of Swarthmore College and the Newhouse School at Syracuse University, Jackson makes his home in North Jersey. He grew up rooting for the Red Sox, Patriots, and Warriors, and he recently added the Devils to his sports fandom mosaic. item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox’ magic number is one.
The Rays, armed with the best record in the American League, are 8-2 in their last 10 games, including a 2-1 win Saturday over Boston. Brayan Bello gave the Sox a solid effort, fanning 11 over eight innings of work.
But in Sunday’s series finale, Boston can clinch a playoff berth. It’s simple: Just win. That’s the easiest option. If Boston loses today, a loss by the Astros seals a date in the postseason. Houston plays the Braves Sunday with first pitch at 2:10 p.m.
Patrick Sandoval will start for the Red Sox Sunday. He has gone six innings just once in his last six starts. He has allowed four runs in his last two starts. He has faced Tampa Bay once this season, surrendering four earned runs in five innings on July 18.
Here’s a preview of Sunday’s action.
Lineups
RED SOX (84-71): Anthony LF, Gasper DH, Rutschman C, Story SS, Sogard 1B, Durbin 3B, Duran CF, Kiner-Falefa 2B, Eaton RF
Pitching: LHP Patrick Sandoval (1-6, 4.99 ERA)
RAYS (94-60): Diaz DH, Vilade 1B, Caminero 3B, DeLuca CF, Simpson LF, Williamson 2B, Fortes C, Mesa Jr. RF, Walls SS
Pitching: RHP Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA)
Time: 1:40 p.m.
TV, radio: NESN, WEEI-FM 93.7

item.title: [Yardbarker] Boston Red Sox Announce Jarren Duran Move on Sunday
item.dc:creator: Simeon Kotto
item.description: The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory. Left-hander Patrick Sandoval takes the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, a matchup that carries extra weight with the regular season winding down and playoff positioning still in flux. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval takes the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, a matchup that carries extra weight with the regular season winding down and playoff positioning still in flux.
Interim manager Chad Tracy has kept the bulk of his starting nine intact, but he has made a modest yet noticeable adjustment involving outfielder Jarren Duran, via Underdog MLB.
After sitting out the series opener and batting eighth on Saturday, Duran will slide up one spot into the seventh hole. He will hit in front of Isaiah Kiner-Falefa and Nate Eaton while remaining in center field, the position he has occupied since injuries to Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White opened the job.
The rest of the order features Roman Anthony in left, Mickey Gasper at designated hitter, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Trevor Story at shortstop, Nick Sogard at first, and Cooper Durbin at third.
The move comes during a difficult individual season for Duran. Entering Sunday he is hitting .206 in 144 games, with 65 runs, 110 hits, 20 home runs and 69 RBIs. His slugging percentage sits at .364 and his OPS at .626.
Speculation about a possible trade lingered for weeks before the August 4 deadline, yet Duran remained in a Red Sox uniform and has continued to receive regular playing time as the club pushes toward October.
Boston sits at 84-71 with seven games left and occupies what currently looks like the second American League Wild Card spot. Should the standings hold, the Red Sox would open the postseason on the road in a best-of-three Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.
Every remaining game, including Sunday’s finale against a familiar division rival, therefore carries playoff implications.
Tracy’s decision to bump Duran up in the order is a small tactical shift rather than a wholesale overhaul, but it signals a willingness to tinker as the club tries to generate more consistent offense down the stretch.
Whether the extra spot in the lineup produces results remains to be seen.
Duran’s season-long struggles have been well documented, yet he has shown flashes of the power and speed that once made him a fixture in the middle of Boston’s order.
A productive afternoon against Jax and the Rays would give the Red Sox a series victory and a bit of momentum heading into the final week.
With the calendar now late September and the postseason picture still taking shape, even incremental lineup changes can feel significant.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have split the first two games of their series with the Tampa Bay Rays.
This now sets up an intriguing rubber match to take place on Sunday afternoon at Tropicana Field as the two teams meet for the final time this regular season.
Ahead of the matchup, the Red Sox got some very encouraging news down in Triple-A Worcester regarding one of their handful of injured pitchers.
Red Sox Get Update on Kutter Crawford
It’s been a whirlwind two-year span for right-handed pitcher Kutter Crawford.
njuries have forced him to battle through setbacks, and after three consistent years with the Red Sox, he hasn’t pitched for the team since 2024.
Crawford missed the entire 2025 season due to knee issues and right wrist surgery. He then opened the 2026 season on the injured list, and while he returned on April 11 to make a rehab start, he immediately went back on the shelf afterward.
Now, WooSox reporter Tommy Cassell has revealed that Crawford will make a rehab appearance for Worcester on Sunday, if the game takes place.
Via Tommy Cassell: “Red Sox pitcher Kutter Crawford is scheduled to make a rehab appearance and pitch today for the WooSox (if they play). The 30-year-old right-hander hasn’t pitched since April 11, which was also a rehab outing with Triple-A Worcester.”
Red Sox pitcher Kutter Crawford is scheduled to make a rehab appearance and pitch today for the WooSox (if they play).
The 30-year-old right-hander hasn’t pitched since April 11, which was also a rehab outing with Triple-A Worcester.
— Tommy Cassell (@TommyCassell_) September 20, 2026
Looking at the Red Sox
Boston enters Sunday with an 84-71 overall record, and their focus is beginning to shift toward postseason mode.
For Crawford, making it into any high-leverage spots at the major league level this year would be quite the miracle. However, simply ending the season with some rehab starts under his belt and potentially finding a way onto the Red Sox taxi squad would be a major development for a player who hasn’t had much luck over the last two seasons.
His exact workload for Sunday remains unknown, and he’ll likely need to make at least a few more appearances before the Red Sox even consider calling him up.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Reinstate RHP Tyron Guerrero from 15-Day IL
BOSTON, MA—The Boston Red Sox today reinstated right-handed pitcher Tyron Guerrero from the 15-Day Injured List. To make room, Boston optioned right-handed pitcher Wyatt Olds to Triple-A Worcester.
Guerrero, 35, was placed on the 15-Day Injured List on September 1 with right shoulder inflammation. The right-hander has recorded a 3.26 ERA (14 ER/38.2 IP) with 36 strikeouts in 38 games for Boston this season. He has also posted a 0.92 ERA (2 ER/19.2 IP) with 22 strikeouts in 15 relief outings for Triple-A Worcester this year. Originally signed as an international free agent by the San Diego Padres in May 2010, the Colombia native owns a 5.10 ERA (82 ER/144.2 IP) with 147 strikeouts in 151 career Major League games with the Padres (2016), Miami Marlins (2018-19), and Red Sox (2026).
Olds, 27, has posted a 1.20 ERA (2 ER/15.0 IP) with 20 strikeouts in 13 relief outings for Boston this season, his Major League debut. The right-hander has also posted a 5.33 ERA (30 ER/50.2 IP) with 74 strikeouts in 39 games this year for Worcester. Selected by the Red Sox in the seventh round of the 2021 First-Year Player Draft, the Oklahoma native owns a 5.88 ERA (254 ER/389.0 IP) with 489 strikeouts in 185 career minor league games (42 starts).

item.title: [Over the Monster] Red Sox News & Links: Willson Contreras still struggling with hand injury
item.dc:creator: Dan Secatore
item.description: X-rays on Willson Contreras’s hand were negative, but don’t take that to mean everything is sunshine, rainbows, and Swiss cheese. Contreras’s hand still shows visible bruising and he cannot grip a bat. He hopes to take some initial swings today. “Hand’s still really sore. Woke up feeling a little better,” he said. “I can squeeze a little better than [Friday], but it’s going to take a few days… I’m going to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs.” (Peter Abraham, B
item.content:encoded:
X-rays on Willson Contreras’s hand were negative, but don’t take that to mean everything is sunshine, rainbows, and Swiss cheese. Contreras’s hand still shows visible bruising and he cannot grip a bat. He hopes to take some initial swings today. “Hand’s still really sore. Woke up feeling a little better,” he said. “I can squeeze a little better than [Friday], but it’s going to take a few days… I’m going to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs.” (Peter Abraham, Boston Globe)
Contreras won’t be on the field for a few days, but he’s still in the clubhouse. That wasn’t the case for Roman Anthony, who was sent to Fort Myers during his rehab, where he worked hard to stay connected to the team. “Just staying in touch with them and seeing what they were doing, I think it’s just the relationship we have,” Anthony said. “As a group, we’re all so close. For me, obviously, Fort Myers wasn’t the most ideal situation, but that’s part of it, and I had a good group of guys down there, and up here.” (Tara Sullivan, Boston Globe)
But now that he’s back in the big leagues, it’s time for Roman to start producing more consistently. He did some extra hitting work before this series against the Rays began and the team is confident he’s going to really get going. “I mean, you see what he can do. It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows,” said Chad Tracy. “He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. Then he went through some stuff, and now he’s starting to look good again. When he’s going well, you see the impact he can make.” (Jen McCaffrey, The Athletic)
Garrett Crochet isn’t with the time right now, but he’s still trying to get back with them. He donned his full uniform yesterday at Polar Park in Worcester and threw 20 pitches, topping out at 92 MPH. The Sox hope he can throw to live hitters at Fenway later this week. Tanner Houck, meanwhile, threw 3.1 innings for the WooSox in his final rehab appearance. (Ian Browne, MLB.com)
A healthy Crochet and Houck could make for a formidable bridge to the back of the bullpen. And after yesterday’s outstanding start, Brayan Bello has also shown that he’s ready to be a part of the postseason action. “For me, it’s just showing the team that I’m ready for these kind of games,” Bello said. “Also, them giving me the opportunity to pitch today was a good step for that. And I thank them for giving me the confidence and the opportunity to start again.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
If Crochet and Houck do make it back to the roster, hopefully their transition will be as seamless as Trevor Story’s has been. “The point of getting the surgery was to come back and try to be the player that I know I can be,” he said, “and it’s starting to show.” (Hayden Bird, Boston.com)

item.title: [bosoxinjection.com] 5 players who are entering their final days as a member of the Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: The Boston Red Sox roster is about to get a bit more crowded as several players are set to return from the injured list before the end of the season. Additionally, even some players who make the cut and play in October might find themselves looking for new homes this winter for a variety of reasons. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox roster is about to get a bit more crowded as several players are set to return from the injured list before the end of the season. Additionally, even some players who make the cut and play in October might find themselves looking for new homes this winter for a variety of reasons.
One thing the Red Sox have is a solid amount of depth. It's what allowed the club to survive so many injuries and mount a rally after such a horrendous start to the season.
On the flip side, sometimes too much depth is a bad thing. There are only so many roster spots to go around, and at a certain point, Boston needs impact players and not just guys who can hold down the fort in case of emergency.
5 players who are entering their final days as a member of the Red Sox
Masataka Yoshida
We'll start with a controversial one. Getting rid of Masataka Yoshida outright would mean eating $18 million in 2027. Even moving him in a trade would likely result in the Red Sox paying down a good portion of his contract. That doesn't exactly sound like something John Henry would go for.
However, there are just too many reasons why the 33-year-old is no longer worth a roster spot. Injuries have played a major role in Yoshida's Red Sox career. On top of that, it's hard to justify a platoon DH without much power and no defensive ability taking up a roster spot, especially given Boston's outfield logjam. There's a chance he's back from the IL prior to the playoffs starting, but it's hard to see how he fits the postseason roster.
Patrick Sandoval
Patrick Sandoval was a worthwhile dart throw as an injury stash when the Red Sox signed him ahead of the 2025 season. With that said, he's shown that he's not much more than a fifth starter at this point. Boston has an abundance of pitching depth, especially of the left-handed variety, making it a near-certainty that the free-agent-to-be is seeking employment elsewhere this offseason.
Isiah Kiner-Falefa
This is a tough one because, in many ways, Isiah Kiner-Falefa has exceeded expectations this season. The utility infielder is having a career season at the plate and has been a spark plug for Boston. However, does his value hold up as well if his bat falls off more in line with his career averages? There is some intangible value to keeping him around, but it's hard to pony up for a cheerleader when the club has other younger and cheaper options.
Triston Casas
Not technically in a Red Sox uniform due to his litany of injuries, but it's fair to say that Triston Casas' days as a member of the organization are numbered. He can't be counted on to stay healthy. It's unclear what his production would look like after so much time away. Finally, Boston could really do without the headaches. This is a clear non-tender case.
Jahmai Jones
It's starting to become clear why Jahmai Jones never got much of an opportunity to carve out a big league role before 2025. Jones is supposed to mash lefties while playing some outfield and DHing, but for much of the season he's done nothing of the sort. Even his breakout 2025 campaign came over just 150 plate appearances. It's not exactly worth going into arbitration with a player who's failing at executing the one skill he supposedly has.
